Planetary Restoration Archive / Foster + Navi

Bridges between proven repair and communities recovering from conflict

Find trustworthy evidence on restoring land, water, food and wellbeing. Then plan, carefully and together with the people affected, whether something that worked elsewhere could help here.

Explore the evidence Plan a bridge Run a listening session

The evidence rule. Every bridge here is a question, not a promise. It stays a proposal until the community has been consulted, the risks have been checked and the results have been measured. Research shows what happened somewhere else. It cannot prove what will happen here.

Works offline. No accounts. No tracking. Your plans stay on your device.

Illustration: at dawn, points of light drift up from one riverbank and gather into a bridge that reaches the other bank.

Start here

Three ways in, depending on who you are, and one sequence that keeps everyone safer.

I’m part of a community

Read the bridges in plain words (turn on Plain language under Display), run a listening session with the meeting kit, and use the planner’s questions in your own meetings. Your community decides what happens on its land.

Open the meeting kit

I work for an organisation or a funder

Check each source’s evidence strength and limits, answer the readiness check honestly, budget for safeguarding and upkeep, and make the Zero Harm and Anti-Coercion covenant a condition of your support.

Open the planner

I’m a researcher, translator or builder

Every source states its limits, has a hand-checked link and a citation you can copy. All content lives in one editable file, translations are plain language packs, and the code is open under the MIT licence.

Read the methods

Five steps, in this order

  1. Listen first. Ask what people need before offering anything. Hold separate, safe conversations with women, young people, displaced families and others who are often left out.
  2. Check safety. Confirm the land is free of explosive hazards, map what divides and connects people, and make sure nothing can reach armed actors.
  3. Find evidence. Look at what worked elsewhere, how strong that evidence is, and what it cannot tell you.
  4. Start small. Take the bridge’s safer first step, with consent, a complaint route and a plan for upkeep.
  5. Measure and share back. Measure what the community said matters, share results with them first, and change course when needed.

Evidence library

Indigenous and traditional knowledge has value in its own context, without an institutional evidence grade. The planner’s Community knowledge tab supports holder-authorized TK documentation, protocols and cross-references. Choosing not to document knowledge is valid.

Publications from UN agencies, research institutes, standard-setters and peer-reviewed journals. Each entry says what kind of source it is, how strong its evidence is and what it cannot tell you. Sources open on their publishers’ websites and need an internet connection.

Every link was checked on 21 October 2026.

How to read evidence strength
A Strong
Several independent, rigorous studies agree.
B Moderate
A rigorous study, a large-data analysis, or a review of many studies.
C Emerging
Before-and-after results, case studies or programme experience, without a comparison group.
D Untested here
An idea or proposal with no measured results yet in this context. Every bridge starts here.
How-to
Guidance, standards and law tell you how to act well. They are not proof that something works.
Context
Situation reports describe a problem. They do not test solutions.

These grades are editorial labels written for this tool. They are not an independent systematic appraisal. Publication dates are not the dates when impacts were observed.

CEvidence review

Programming for Climate, Peace and Security: Thematic Review and Guidance Note

Reviews 15 climate, peace and security projects across 28 countries, with cases from Africa, Central Asia, the Pacific, Latin America and the Middle East, and turns them into guidance on risk assessment, design, stakeholder engagement and monitoring.

CCase studies

From Crisis to Resilience: Climate Solutions for Positive Peacebuilding

Ten country cases (Colombia, DR Congo, Ghana, Iraq, Jordan, Kenya, the Philippines, Sierra Leone, Timor-Leste and Uzbekistan) showing how climate adaptation, mitigation and finance can support peace in fragile settings, across water, energy, land, livelihoods, gender and data.

UNDP. 14 January 2026.

Keep in mind: Cases were chosen to illustrate approaches. They are not compared with places that had no programme.

How-toPractical guidance

Programme Guidance and Operational Notes: Strengthening Shock-Responsive Social Protection Systems

Updates UNICEF’s 2019 guidance on preparing social protection, including cash transfers, for shocks such as conflict, climate change, displacement and pandemics. Three operational notes cover climate, forced displacement and conflict settings.

UNICEF. 6 July 2026.

Keep in mind: Guidance on how to design systems. It does not measure results.

How-toPractical guidance

Land Restoration From Planting to Proof: A Guide to Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification

A 120-page guidebook, co-created and field-tested with more than 200 locally led restoration projects. It tracks nine biophysical, socioeconomic and financial indicator categories and uses high-resolution satellite imagery with an AI tree-counting model for verification.

World Resources Institute. 12 January 2026.

Keep in mind: Built for restoration portfolios. Satellite and location data need extra privacy protection in conflict settings.

Open sourceLink checked 21 October 2026
BPeer-reviewed study

Armed Conflict Accelerates Cropland Loss and Food Insecurity Worldwide

Combines annual 30-metre global cropland maps (2000–2020) with more than 460,000 conflict events in 155 countries. Using difference-in-differences and propensity score matching, it finds that conflict-affected areas lost 23.7% more cropland than comparable areas, with losses lasting for years.

Nature Food. 24 September 2026.

Keep in mind: One global study of land within 5 km of conflict events. It measures association with careful controls; it cannot explain every local cause.

Open sourceLink checked 21 October 2026
CProgramme evaluation

Building Cross-Border Peace and Strengthening Sustainable Livelihoods of Cattle Herders and Crop Farmers in Sierra Leone and Guinea: Endline Assessment

Endline assessment of a USD 4.55 million project (2021–2024) run by WFP, IOM and Talking Drum Studio with both governments in Falaba (Sierra Leone) and Faranah (Guinea). Households reporting a farmer–herder dispute in the past year fell from 41% to 8.6%, and 96.5% of reported disputes were resolved.

UN Peacebuilding Fund. June 2024.

Keep in mind: A before-and-after survey with no comparison group and some convenience sampling, so not every improvement can be credited to the project.

A two-step assessment for judging the peace potential of climate adaptation work. It checks whether a climate programme fits the conflict context where it operates and recommends changes to improve that fit.

CGIAR (Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT). October 2024.

BEvidence review

The Impact of Violent Conflict on Smallholder Agriculture: A Scoping Review

Maps 85 publications (2000–2024) on how violent conflict harms smallholder farming: destruction and looting of crops, tools and irrigation; theft of livestock; abandonment and displacement; seed insecurity; and broken markets, inputs and labour.

ContextSituation report

Summarises a UNDP and International Trade Centre analysis of Sudan’s farm and market systems since the conflict began in April 2023. How-toPractical guidance

Do No Harm (Local Capacities for Peace) Framework

A widely used way to check how aid and development work affects conflict. It asks what divides people and what connects them, how a project’s actions and staff behaviour strengthen or weaken each, and what small changes would do better.

CDA Collaborative Learning. Since 1993.

Keep in mind: An analysis method. Its value depends on honest, inclusive local analysis, repeated as things change.

Humane, practical support for people after extremely distressing events, built around three action principles (look, listen and link) and centred on people’s dignity, culture and abilities.

WHO, War Trauma Foundation and World Vision International. 2 October 2011.

Keep in mind: Psychological first aid is basic support. It is not counselling or treatment, and it should connect people to specialised care when they need it.

A manual for project practitioners. Consent must be free of coercion, sought before activities begin, informed in local languages and formats, and decided through the community’s own processes, with the right to say yes, no, or yes with conditions, and to withdraw later.

How Niger’s FMNR Experience Has Inspired a Global Scaling Movement

Describes farmer-managed natural regeneration: regrowing trees from living stumps, roots and seeds already in the ground. In Niger an estimated 200 million trees regrew across about 5 million hectares of farmland, spreading mostly from farmer to farmer between the mid-1980s and the mid-2000s.

The Impact of Cash Transfers: A Review of the Evidence from Low- and Middle-Income Countries

Reviews 165 studies (2000–2015) of cash transfers that recipients do not pay into, across six areas: monetary poverty, education, health and nutrition, savings and production, work, and empowerment. Rebuilding Resilience in the Sahel: Regreening in the Maradi and Zinder Regions of Niger

A systems analysis of regreening across more than 5 million hectares in the Maradi and Zinder regions over two decades. It finds no single cause: decline reversed when governance changed first, then livelihoods, and then the land itself.

Zai or Tassa Planting Pits (Niger)

Field documentation of zaï pits: about 10,000 small pits per hectare, dug across the slope and filled with compost, to catch rain and nutrients and bring degraded land back into use. Plots with pits and fertiliser averaged 409 kg of millet per hectare, against 195 kg on control plots.

WOCAT (World Overview of Conservation Approaches and Technologies). July 2012.

Keep in mind: Field records and the compilers’ estimates, not a controlled trial. Heavy labour can exclude households short of workers.

ContextSituation report

Household Air Pollution

About 2.1 billion people cook with open fires or inefficient stoves burning wood, dung, charcoal, coal or kerosene. Household air pollution caused an estimated 2.9 million deaths in 2021, including over 309,000 children under five. Women and children bear the greatest burden.

World Health Organization. 16 December 2025.

How-toPractical guidance

SAFE: Safe Access to Fuel and Energy

Explains why cooking fuel is a protection issue in displacement: women and girls risk rape, beatings and killings while collecting firewood, camps strip nearby land and strain relations with host communities, and families sometimes sell food to buy fuel. It sets out the SAFE approach of assessing energy needs and risks and pressing for policy change.

Women’s Refugee Commission. 2014.

Keep in mind: A 2014 advocacy fact sheet. Its figures date from then.

BEvidence review

Impacts of School Feeding on Educational and Health Outcomes of School-Age Children and Adolescents in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

Reviews 57 studies (44 randomised trials and 13 controlled before-and-after studies). School feeding increased the share of school days attended by 2.6%, and over 12 months raised weight by 0.58 kg and height by 0.32 cm compared with control groups.

Journal of Global Health. 4 September 2021.

Keep in mind: Most included studies had a high risk of bias, and effects on learning and nutrition need better research.

Open sourceLink checked 21 October 2026
BListening study

Time to Listen: Hearing People on the Receiving End of International Aid

Based on conversations with nearly 6,000 people in 20 countries over five years. People generally appreciated aid but said it was not achieving its purpose: very few asked for more aid, most wanted smarter aid that builds on local capacity, and many felt too much came too fast.

CDA Collaborative Learning. November 2012.

Keep in mind: Qualitative listening, not a measurement of programme effects.

Evidence web

Which sources each bridge rests on. Lines take the colour of the source’s evidence strength. Point at, tap or tab to a bridge to trace its sources; select a source to jump to it in the library.

Explore institutional evidence connections and locally mapped relationships among water, food, education, health, land rights, governance, women leadership, youth participation and restoration. Proposed pathways can connect Water → School Attendance → Social Stability → Reduced Tension; they are hypotheses to examine locally.

Solution bridges

Proposed pathways from documented experience to communities that ask for help. None of them is an existing partnership or a funded project. Each one needs an independent conflict and ecological risk assessment and the community’s free, prior and informed consent.

Community seed sovereignty, seed banks and local propagation

Rebuild locally governed seed reserves and nursery capacity, with transparent stock records, diverse locally chosen varieties and documented rights to use and exchange material.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Category: Seed Sovereignty & Local Propagation

Where it comes from

A proposed pathway informed by FAO community seed-bank guidance, farmer seed systems and community-led stewardship. Open-source pledges are distinct from community-controlled access.

Who it could help

Growers rebuilding agricultural livelihoods after disrupted seed supplies, while retaining control over diversity, knowledge and propagation decisions.

What must be true first

  • Community authorization and inclusive stewardship roles, including women, youth and displaced growers.
  • Safe land and access verified through the Hazard & Demining prerequisite before any field or nursery intervention.
  • Locally appropriate varieties, seed/plant health review and documented permissions or transfer terms.
  • Reliable water, storage, containers, tools and an owned contingency for each critical supply.

What could go wrong

  • Stock and location records expose vulnerable banks or custodians.
  • Donated seed is mistakenly declared open source or distributed against community protocols.
  • Poor seed health, unsuitable varieties or disrupted water undermine propagation.
  • Elite capture, coercive repayment or dependence on one supplier weakens sovereignty.

How to prevent harm

  • Keep records local and omit exact locations and identities; use encrypted backups when appropriate.
  • Record actual permission and pledge/license obligations; no automatic legal or quality certification.
  • Keep lots and units separate, record review expiry and use hazard prerequisites before field activity.
  • Review access and benefit-sharing with affected growers; retain diverse varieties and realistic fallbacks.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Convene willing seed stewards to agree one non-sensitive inventory pilot, community permissions, quality review and safe access prerequisites.

How a pilot could start

  • Agree community governance, access rules, attribution and non-coercive replenishment expectations.
  • Create separate lots for each variety, source and unit; document provenance and permission.
  • Review seed or planting-material quality with appropriate local expertise and record method, sample and uncertainty.
  • Record receipts, issues, losses and corrections without overwriting history.
  • Track nursery units started, established, surviving and ready; verify outputs before recording stock.
  • Review shortages, distribution fairness, diversity loss and maintenance needs; adapt through community decisions.

What to measure

  • Stock balances and documented losses by lot and unit.
  • Germination or establishment and survival with explicit denominators and method.
  • Variety diversity and voluntary grower preferences, including reasons for rejection.
  • Supply gaps with owner roles, confidence, verification and contingencies.
  • Participation in seed decisions and fair access, assessed separately from yield or peace claims.

Conceptual / Proposed locally. The register supports stewardship and learning; it does not certify seed quality, legal permissions, ecological suitability or peace outcomes.

Evidence behind this bridge

  • Community seed banks: Junior Farmer Field and Life School – Facilitator’s guide
  • CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance
  • Free Prior and Informed Consent: An Indigenous Peoples’ Right and a Good Practice for Local Communities
  • Do No Harm (Local Capacities for Peace) Framework

Shared watersheds: upstream and downstream cooperation

Bring willing water users together to understand a shared watershed, agree small restoration tasks and review how benefits and burdens are distributed.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Category: Restoration Diplomacy

Where it comes from

A proposed cooperation pathway informed by the UN World Water Development Report and conflict-sensitive resource governance guidance.

Who it could help

Upstream and downstream communities seeking fairer cooperation around erosion, water retention, water quality and seasonal access.

What must be true first

  • Voluntary participation from upstream and downstream users, including less powerful and seasonally absent groups.
  • Trusted facilitation, relevant basin institutions and clarity about each participant’s authority.
  • An agreed baseline, ecological advice and resources for maintenance and dialogue.

What could go wrong

  • Upstream interventions shift costs downstream or reduce access for other users.
  • Dominant users control the discussion and present consultation as consent.
  • Seasonal rainfall changes are mistaken for project effects.
  • A technical agreement is interpreted as deciding water rights or territorial claims.

How to prevent harm

  • Include affected users on all sides and review distribution of benefits and burdens.
  • Do not treat this plan as authority to allocate water rights or change existing agreements.
  • Compare seasons and document uncertainty; seek appropriate hydrological advice before physical works.
  • Allow separate feedback, refusal and independent review when parties disagree.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Hold facilitated listening sessions with willing upstream and downstream groups, then agree one reversible erosion-monitoring or maintenance trial with a review date.

How a pilot could start

  • Listen separately to different users before a joint discussion; record priorities and disagreements without identifying individuals.
  • Describe the shared water problem at a broad scale and distinguish observations from contested claims.
  • Agree a small restoration action, responsibilities, cost sharing and how downstream effects will be reviewed.
  • Set common observation methods and seasonal comparison periods; include water access and ecological effects.
  • Establish a complaint route, drought review trigger and a process for revising unfair arrangements.
  • Review ecological changes and whether cooperation continued through disagreement before extending the agreement.

What to measure

  • Water retention or soil cover measured with a shared method and comparable seasonal baseline.
  • Agreed maintenance tasks completed by each participating group, with reasons for delay.
  • Participation and meaningful influence of upstream, downstream and underrepresented users.
  • Disputes addressed through the agreed process, distinguishing unresolved cases from mutually accepted resolution.
  • Voluntary trust feedback and perceived fairness of water access, including dissent.

An exploratory Restoration Diplomacy pathway. Ecological cooperation may support peacebuilding, but outcomes depend on power, rights, context and sustained relationships. Start at Conceptual / Proposed and assess ecological and peace outcomes separately.

Evidence behind this bridge

  • Do No Harm (Local Capacities for Peace) Framework
  • Voluntary Guidelines on the Responsible Governance of Tenure of Land, Fisheries and Forests (VGGT)

Shared seed systems: reciprocal learning and diversity

Connect willing seed stewards across communities to exchange learning, support locally adapted diversity and negotiate fair arrangements for any permitted seed sharing.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Category: Restoration Diplomacy

Where it comes from

A proposed intercommunity cooperation pathway informed by FAO community seed-bank guidance and community-controlled knowledge principles.

Who it could help

Communities who want reciprocal support for seed diversity while respecting local preferences, seed health and knowledge-holder authority.

What must be true first

  • Seed stewards and growers who choose to participate, including women and youth with meaningful decision roles.
  • Local agronomic support, seed-quality checks and clear rules for access, benefit sharing and knowledge reuse.
  • Confirmation of applicable requirements before any seed movement, especially across borders.

What could go wrong

  • Seed movement spreads pests or introduces unsuitable material.
  • Exchange rules override farmers’ preferences or knowledge-holder rights.
  • A failed harvest creates debt, blame or obligations that deepen tension.
  • Benefits concentrate with established seed traders or powerful stewards.

How to prevent harm

  • Start with learning exchange; move material only after appropriate technical and regulatory checks.
  • Respect local diversity, farmers’ choices and permission for knowledge reuse.
  • Use transparent, voluntary arrangements with agreed crop-failure provisions.
  • Assess who gains access and who bears storage, transport and care costs.

Smaller, safer first step

Convene a voluntary exchange of seed-stewardship knowledge; agree a small, technically reviewed trial only if all relevant permissions and safeguards are satisfied.

How a pilot could start

  • Compare seed needs and local growing conditions without assuming that varieties suitable in one place suit another.
  • Begin with knowledge exchange and agree what information and material may be shared.
  • Have qualified partners review seed health, suitability and applicable movement requirements before an exchange.
  • Trial small permitted quantities with voluntary growers and retain diverse local options.
  • Agree fair access, storage, replenishment and responses to crop failure without coercive repayment.
  • Review germination, access, reciprocal support and disagreements with all participating groups.

What to measure

  • Locally preferred varieties accessible to participating growers, with gaps recorded.
  • Germination and survival for each trial cohort, with conditions and failures reported.
  • Fair access and decision influence of women, youth and less-resourced growers.
  • Reciprocal learning or support commitments completed and maintained across seasons.
  • Disagreements about access or obligations resolved by mutual agreement, alongside voluntary trust feedback.

Cross-border restoration: cooperating across shared landscapes

Help willing communities and authorized institutions coordinate restoration across an ecological landscape while respecting jurisdiction, tenure and different local priorities.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Category: Restoration Diplomacy

Where it comes from

An exploratory pathway informed by UNCCD’s Peace Forest Initiative and ecosystem restoration principles.

Who it could help

Communities and institutions seeking complementary restoration efforts across administrative or national boundaries.

What must be true first

  • Community mandates and authorized institutional partners on each side, with agreed limits to their roles.
  • Tenure and access review, appropriate ecological expertise and a conflict-sensitive feasibility assessment.
  • A shared maintenance and benefit-sharing plan that can continue despite funding or leadership changes.

What could go wrong

  • Restoration is used to assert territorial or tenure claims.
  • Access restrictions exclude customary users or displace livelihoods.
  • Visible collaboration exposes participants to retaliation or political pressure.
  • Different resources or funding cycles create unequal obligations and abandoned maintenance.

How to prevent harm

  • Do not imply recognition of boundaries or settle territorial claims through a project plan.
  • Confirm local consent, land rights and necessary permissions with appropriate partners.
  • Use broad-area summaries and allow safe separate or remote participation.
  • Agree pause criteria, independent review and funded maintenance before scaling.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

With willing communities and authorized partners, compare existing non-sensitive restoration priorities and design two small complementary pilots with shared review criteria.

How a pilot could start

  • Clarify mandates, community priorities and unresolved tenure concerns before defining a joint activity.
  • Agree complementary ecological objectives and document where priorities differ.
  • Choose a modest pilot with appropriate permissions; parallel activities can begin without crossing a border.
  • Agree responsibilities, costs, maintenance and an accessible process for concerns.
  • Use comparable monitoring while keeping sensitive locations and personal records out of shared reports.
  • Review ecological outcomes, benefit distribution and continuity of dialogue; pause or adapt if activities increase tension.

What to measure

  • Trees surviving, soil cover or biodiversity observations using agreed cohort and sampling methods.
  • Maintenance commitments completed on each side and outstanding resource gaps.
  • Distribution of benefits and access restrictions reported by different user groups.
  • Joint projects sustained through a review cycle, not merely announced.
  • Continuity of dialogue during disagreement, voluntary trust indicators and unresolved concerns.

Joint monitoring: shared observation and accountable interpretation

Create a jointly agreed way to observe ecological change, compare interpretations and use findings for shared decisions without turning monitoring into surveillance.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Category: Restoration Diplomacy

Where it comes from

A proposed cooperation workflow informed by restoration principles, accountability and environmental peacebuilding guidance.

Who it could help

Groups who share ecological concerns but lack trusted observations or disagree about what existing measurements mean.

What must be true first

  • An agreed question, representative monitoring roles and voluntary participation.
  • Comparable methods, calibrated tools where needed and a budget for training and repeat observations.
  • Data permissions, review responsibilities and a safe route to contest interpretations.

What could go wrong

  • Different sampling effort produces misleading comparisons and accusations.
  • Monitoring identifies vulnerable people, sensitive sites or resource users.
  • One partner controls instruments, interpretation or publication.
  • Jointly signed data is mistaken for proof of peace or universal agreement.

How to prevent harm

  • Agree methods in advance and report missing data, calibration limits and alternative explanations.
  • Collect only necessary ecological data; omit precise sensitive locations and personal identifiers.
  • Give all partners a meaningful review role and preserve contested interpretations.
  • Separate ecological findings from claims about trust or reduced conflict; allow withdrawal from participation.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Agree one non-sensitive indicator, compare observations from two voluntary teams, and discuss measurement differences before publishing any joint conclusion.

How a pilot could start

  • Choose one ecological question and agree what decisions the observations could inform.
  • Define a baseline, units, sampling effort, observation dates and how missing data will be recorded.
  • Train observers from participating groups and compare measurements on a non-sensitive trial sample.
  • Record uncertainty and disagreements; retain an audit trail when correcting data.
  • Interpret results together and allow separate accounts when agreement is not reached.
  • Share only approved summaries and review whether findings changed decisions or strengthened cooperation.

What to measure

  • Observations meeting the agreed method divided by observations attempted, including missing samples.
  • Differences between observers and the proportion examined through joint review.
  • Corrections documented and contested interpretations retained.
  • Shared decisions that explicitly used findings, with reasons and follow-up dates.
  • Connector institutions’ review and response capacity, alongside voluntary accounts of trust and fairness.

An exploratory Restoration Diplomacy pathway. Ecological cooperation may support peacebuilding, but outcomes depend on power, rights, context and sustained relationships. Start at Conceptual / Proposed and assess ecological and peace outcomes separately.

Offline education hubs: learning through connection gaps

Create a locally maintained learning hub with useful lessons available without a continuing Internet connection, supported by educators and accessible non-digital alternatives.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Category: Digital Peace Infrastructure

Where it comes from

A proposed community learning pathway informed by Learning Equality’s Kolibri approach and existing accountability guidance.

Who it could help

Learners and educators who request dependable access to learning material where connectivity is costly or intermittent.

What must be true first

  • Community and educator agreement on learning priorities, languages and suitable content rights.
  • Maintainable devices, local storage, safe power and a budget for repair and replacement.
  • Facilitators with time to support learners; accessible materials and fair device-sharing arrangements.

What could go wrong

  • Devices or charging costs exclude the people the hub is intended to serve.
  • Inappropriate or outdated material displaces local teaching priorities.
  • Learner records expose children or become a basis for ranking groups.
  • Hardware breaks after initial funding ends; educators inherit unpaid maintenance work.

How to prevent harm

  • Use inclusive scheduling and accessible formats; never make device ownership a condition of learning.
  • Keep identifiable learner records out of this planner and shared exports.
  • Obtain appropriate content permissions and community review before distribution.
  • Maintain a repair budget, supported educators and a non-digital fallback; never assume an offline platform includes all content.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Trial one locally chosen lesson with a small voluntary group, disconnect the Internet, and review usability, learning support and access barriers before buying more equipment.

How a pilot could start

  • Agree learning goals with educators, caregivers and learners using age-appropriate participation.
  • Review a small, licensed content collection for language, accessibility, relevance and accuracy.
  • Prepare the local hub and test lessons with the Internet disconnected; document which functions still need a connection.
  • Trial a fair access schedule with supported sessions and printed or spoken alternatives.
  • Train at least two maintenance roles, test backup recovery and schedule content reviews.
  • Review learning progress and exclusion with participants before extending the hub.

What to measure

  • Sessions successfully completed offline divided by sessions attempted, with period and failure reasons.
  • Voluntary participation rate using an agreed eligible population and recording access barriers.
  • Aggregate learning-goal completion against a baseline; do not equate screen time with learning.
  • School attendance where appropriate, using school-open days and comparable periods.
  • Repair downtime, maintenance costs and number of supported local maintenance roles.

A proposed Digital Peace Infrastructure pathway, not a locally tested intervention. Guidance supports design choices but does not establish peace impacts. Begin at Conceptual / Proposed; record local observations and review before changing maturity.

Community archives: preserving shared memory with consent

Build a community-governed archive of restoration histories, practices and shared learning, with clear rules about what may be kept, who may access it and what may be shared.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Category: Digital Peace Infrastructure

Where it comes from

A proposed archival pathway informed by UNESCO documentary heritage guidance and, where relevant, Indigenous data governance principles.

Who it could help

Communities wishing to preserve memory across generations and steward material that they choose to retain.

What must be true first

  • A community-selected stewardship group and consent process respecting knowledge-holder authority.
  • A minimal catalogue, accessible formats, suitable storage and tested backup arrangements.
  • Agreed access, retention, correction, withdrawal and succession rules before collection begins.

What could go wrong

  • Public preservation exposes sacred knowledge, private experiences or contested histories.
  • Copies circulate beyond agreed audiences and cannot reliably be recalled.
  • A single custodian, device or proprietary format becomes a point of failure.
  • One group’s account is presented as the only legitimate community history.

How to prevent harm

  • Allow refusal and non-recording; public benefit does not override knowledge-holder permissions.
  • Separate public descriptions from restricted source material; this planner is not a secure archive repository.
  • Preserve differing accounts with context and uncertainty; provide correction and withdrawal routes.
  • Test readable recovery and format migration; explain limits on withdrawing already distributed copies.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Co-design a catalogue for three non-sensitive, voluntarily offered items; agree access and retention, then restore a test copy before collecting further material.

How a pilot could start

  • Agree the archive purpose and identify material that must remain unrecorded or restricted.
  • Trial a small collection with permission for recording, storage, access and reuse treated as separate decisions.
  • Catalogue broad context, language, provenance, permissions and review dates without sensitive identifying details.
  • Maintain at least two appropriately protected copies on separate media and test restoration.
  • Offer accessible listening or reading sessions and invite corrections without forcing disclosure.
  • Review access and retention with knowledge holders and hand over stewardship through a documented process.

What to measure

  • Items with explicit access and reuse permission divided by items retained.
  • Successful restore checks and time needed to recover a usable copy.
  • Requested corrections or withdrawals addressed by the agreed review date.
  • Languages and accessible formats available, with gaps identified by participants.
  • Voluntary accounts of whether stewardship represents different groups fairly.

A proposed Digital Peace Infrastructure pathway, not a locally tested intervention. Guidance supports design choices but does not establish peace impacts. Begin at Conceptual / Proposed; record local observations and review before changing maturity.

Local knowledge systems: community evidence in its own context

Maintain a community-reviewed collection of observations, lessons and unexpected outcomes in local languages, preserving context and the authority of people who share knowledge.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Category: Digital Peace Infrastructure

Where it comes from

A proposed learning pathway informed by community listening and the CARE Principles where Indigenous knowledge and data are involved.

Who it could help

Restoration groups and communities who want local experience to inform decisions without losing control of their knowledge.

What must be true first

  • Knowledge holders who choose whether and how to participate; recognition of relevant collective authority.
  • Facilitators or interpreters, accessible formats and a process for disagreement and corrections.
  • Local custodians, review dates and permission rules for exchange with other communities.

What could go wrong

  • Translation removes local meaning or implies agreement that was never given.
  • Knowledge is extracted for outsiders’ benefit without reciprocal value.
  • A vivid account is mistaken for replicated evidence or universal best practice.
  • Restricted knowledge is copied into public exports or loses its provenance.

How to prevent harm

  • Respect individual and collective authority and Indigenous data governance where applicable.
  • Record uncertainty and dissent; examples are prompts, not findings.
  • Keep sharing local by default and review permission for every revised account.
  • Return useful findings to contributors and preserve context rather than ranking communities.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Invite a voluntary group to review one non-sensitive restoration observation in its own language, record uncertainty and decide whether it should remain local.

How a pilot could start

  • Agree a practical learning question and what knowledge should not be recorded.
  • Capture observations, lessons and unexpected outcomes with broad context, period, method and limitations.
  • Return accounts to contributors in their preferred language and record differing interpretations.
  • Link learning to relevant bridge, impact indicator and proposed system relationship without automatically claiming causation.
  • Share only approved summaries through existing knowledge exchange; retain provenance and revise permissions after changes.
  • Review what changed in practice and whether contributors benefited; withdraw or correct material when needed.

What to measure

  • Accounts returned to contributors for review divided by accounts recorded.
  • Approved summaries with context, method and limitations recorded.
  • Corrections incorporated and disagreements retained without identifying individuals.
  • Community decisions informed by learning, with an explanation of how it was used.
  • Voluntary trust and perceived-benefit feedback, including missing perspectives.

Mesh communication: locally governed connection pathways

Explore a maintainable local communication network that can connect community services across nearby nodes, with realistic coverage, power, privacy and operating expectations.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Category: Digital Peace Infrastructure

Where it comes from

A proposed local networking pathway informed by Internet Society’s community-network planning toolkit. Mesh is one possible topology, not a universal solution.

Who it could help

Communities that request local communication or access to shared learning resources during unreliable connectivity.

What must be true first

  • A community mandate and a qualified local technical partner to assess suitability and applicable requirements.
  • A clear service scope: local resource access, messaging or Internet connection are different capabilities.
  • Lifecycle funding for power, repairs, updates and trained operators, with agreed ownership and access rules.

What could go wrong

  • Terrain, interference or node failure prevents reliable coverage.
  • Power and replacement costs exceed the community’s maintenance capacity.
  • Traffic or device identifiers expose users; connectivity is mistaken for secure communication.
  • Dependence on a pilot creates false confidence during emergencies.

How to prevent harm

  • Use qualified installation and current local requirements; do not publish node locations or security configurations in shared plans.
  • State tested limits and distinguish local reach from Internet connectivity.
  • Minimize traffic logging and review security before any sensitive use.
  • Keep established fallback channels and avoid promises of emergency availability.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

With qualified support, test one agreed non-sensitive local service on a small authorized network; document failure conditions and who will maintain it before expansion.

How a pilot could start

  • Agree the intended service and compare mesh with simpler local networking or non-digital options.
  • Have a qualified partner assess feasibility, applicable radio requirements and permissions before installation.
  • Choose equipment for maintainability and test a small authorized pilot with non-sensitive traffic.
  • Test power loss, node failure and Internet disconnection; record actual service limits.
  • Review privacy, authentication, software updates and safe operator handover; do not assume mesh means encryption.
  • Practise fallback communication and review costs, exclusion and reliability before expanding.

What to measure

  • Successful test messages or resource requests divided by attempts during a defined test period.
  • Service availability during planned tests, with power and node failures recorded.
  • Recovery time and unresolved maintenance tasks after a simulated outage.
  • Operating and replacement costs compared with committed funds.
  • Access barriers and voluntary user feedback; avoid identifying traffic logs.

Resilience information portals: trusted information through disruption

Organize locally relevant restoration and service information in an accessible portal with offline copies, clear source dates, correction routes and a plan for outdated information.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Category: Digital Peace Infrastructure

Where it comes from

A proposed information-stewardship workflow informed by community accountability and listening guidance, alongside community-network planning resources.

Who it could help

Communities seeking a dependable place to find agreed public information when connectivity and service availability change.

What must be true first

  • Trusted editorial roles and a source-verification and correction process.
  • A deliberately limited public information scope, local languages and accessible offline formats.
  • Update responsibilities, review dates, distribution channels and a fallback when information cannot be verified.

What could go wrong

  • An old offline copy is mistaken for current service or hazard information.
  • Rumours or unverified claims acquire authority through the portal.
  • A portal excludes people who cannot read its language or use its devices.
  • Publishing personal contacts or sensitive locations exposes people; maintainers become overloaded.

How to prevent harm

  • Use verified public information and clearly separate uncertainty from confirmed updates.
  • Show dates and expiry prominently; direct time-critical questions to established local channels.
  • Publish no private contacts, precise sensitive locations or individual case records.
  • Maintain accessible alternatives and named collective editorial roles with succession and correction responsibilities.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Trial a small page of non-sensitive information, ask residents to find and understand it offline, and practise correcting an expired item across all trial copies.

  • Ask residents which non-sensitive information is useful and which channels they can actually access.
  • Agree sources, editorial responsibilities and how conflicting or unverified information is handled.
  • Publish concise entries with source, last-verified date, review or expiry date and an accessible correction route.
  • Test offline copies and clearly label their age; remove or flag expired information instead of presenting it as current.
  • Provide print or spoken alternatives and a procedure for circulating corrections across copies.
  • Review usefulness, missing audiences and update workload with residents before adding more content.

  • Published entries reviewed within their agreed interval divided by entries due for review.
  • Time from verified correction to replacement of distributed copies where reachable.
  • Successful information-finding tasks in each offered language or format.

  • Outdated entries found in spot checks and unresolved information gaps.

Regenerative Governance: shared decisions and accountable stewardship

Agree how people make decisions, allocate shared resources, oversee ecological care and challenge unfair choices, so projects can survive leadership changes and disputes.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Category: Regenerative Governance

Where it comes from

A proposed local combination of participatory budgeting, community assemblies, stewardship councils and transparent decision-making. OECD participation guidance and existing restoration, accountability and conflict-sensitivity sources inform the design; this combined bridge has not been tested locally.

Who it could help

Communities planning or maintaining shared water, food, restoration or other projects, especially where unclear authority, exclusion, disputed budgets or unaccountable leadership threaten continuity.

What must be true first

  • A voluntary community mandate defining which decisions are genuinely open, who holds resources, and who can pause or revise the process.
  • An affected-groups map, including women, young people, displaced people, customary users and people who cannot attend meetings; participation must be accessible and safe.
  • Agreement with existing legitimate institutions about the scope of the process, without treating a new council as a substitute for rights or an elected authority.
  • A realistic resource envelope and maintenance commitment; no consultation about funds or choices that participants cannot actually influence.
  • A trusted complaint and appeal route outside the immediate decision-makers, with confidential options and no retaliation.

What could go wrong

  • Elite capture: established leaders or funders control proposals, information or representative selection.
  • Token participation: assemblies are held after decisions have already been made, or participants lack real authority.
  • Majority decisions override minority access, tenure or other rights; attendance is mistaken for consent.
  • Opaque procurement, undeclared conflicts of interest or maintenance money diverted from its agreed purpose.
  • Meeting fatigue, unpaid work and inaccessible formats disproportionately burden women, youth or people with disabilities.
  • A stewardship council becomes permanent, cannot be removed, or competes with existing institutions.
  • Public records expose complainants or create retaliation risks; a low complaint count is mistaken for trust.

How to prevent harm

  • Publish the scope of authority and available resources before inviting proposals; distinguish decisions from advice and feedback.
  • Provide multiple accessible participation routes and meaningful decision power; do not equate a seat or attendance with influence.
  • Agree representation, quorum, recusal, term limits, recall and succession rules before appointing a council.
  • Publish aggregate budgets and decision reasons in formats people can use, while withholding personal complaints and sensitive identities.
  • Protect dissent and refusal; keep an independent appeal route and review unresolved concerns without compulsory disclosure.
  • Do not treat a vote or this planning tool as legal authorization, proof of consent, or authority to alter land rights.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

With community agreement, trial one reversible maintenance decision using a small disclosed resource envelope. Record the options, participation barriers, chosen criteria, rationale and review date; evaluate the process before expanding its mandate.

How a pilot could start

  • Participatory budgeting: agree a small, real allocation, eligibility rules and public assessment criteria; invite proposals and cost maintenance before choosing priorities.
  • Community assemblies: share options in accessible local formats, allow small-group and non-meeting input, record disagreement and agree quorum and decision rules before deliberation.
  • Stewardship councils: choose accountable representatives by a community-agreed process; define duties, term lengths, rotation, removal, succession and a review date.
  • Transparent decision-making: record the options, criteria, reasons, declared interests, recusals, responsible collective role and review date; explain proposals not selected.
  • Separate proposal selection, spending approval and expenditure checking where feasible; reconcile planned and actual costs in the existing budget and share an aggregate account.
  • Use the consent log for conditions and concerns, the risk register for exclusion or retaliation, and the timeline for budget reviews, council rotation and maintenance handover.
  • Hold a return meeting to examine participation, decisions implemented, unresolved concerns and ecological consequences; revise rules when the process excludes people.
  • Pause contested or coercive decisions, protect confidential feedback, and seek an agreed independent review before continuing.

What to measure

  • Participation rate: participants divided by the locally agreed eligible population, with accessible non-meeting contributions counted consistently.
  • Women and youth in roles with actual decision authority, alongside their own accounts of whether they influenced outcomes.
  • Share of the agreed budget decided through the process, and planned versus actual expenditure with explanations for variance.
  • Proportion of decisions with accessible reasons and a recorded response to objections; time taken to report back.
  • Stewardship actions completed by their agreed review date and maintenance obligations still unfunded.
  • Community trust indicators gathered voluntarily, with limitations and missing perspectives reported.
  • Concerns raised, response time and outcomes; distinguish unresolved concerns from resolved disputes and never interpret fewer complaints alone as success.

Implementation guidance and a proposed local workflow, not a causal claim that assemblies, budgeting or councils prevent project failure. Start at Conceptual / Proposed and update maturity only after a documented local review.

Evidence behind this bridge

  • OECD Guidelines for Citizen Participation Processes
  • Principles for Ecosystem Restoration to Guide the United Nations Decade 2021–2030
  • Core Humanitarian Standard on Quality and Accountability (2024 edition)
  • Do No Harm (Local Capacities for Peace) Framework
  • Voluntary Guidelines on the Responsible Governance of Tenure of Land, Fisheries and Forests (VGGT)
  • Time to Listen: Hearing People on the Receiving End of International Aid

Farmer-managed natural regeneration for land and livelihood recovery

Help trees regrow from living stumps and roots already in farmers’ fields, so tired land recovers at low cost and families gain shade, fodder, firewood and better harvests.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Where it comes from

Farmer-led regreening in Niger, where an estimated 200 million trees regrew across about 5 million hectares of farmland, spreading from farmer to farmer over two decades. An analysis of the Maradi and Zinder regions found that the turnaround began with changes in governance, then livelihoods, and only then the land.

Who it could help

Degraded farmland where living stumps and roots remain, where the community has asked for support, and where the people doing the work can keep the benefits of the trees.

What must be true first

  • Clear, fair agreement on who owns and benefits from regrown trees, including women and tenant farmers.
  • Agreement with herders on grazing, livestock corridors and dry-season access.
  • Confirmation from a mine action authority that the land is safe to work, wherever fighting took place.
  • Rainfall, soil and rootstock that can support regrowth, checked with local knowledge.

What could go wrong

  • Disputes over who owns regrown trees, or land grabs as land values rise.
  • Blocked livestock routes that raise farmer–herder tension.
  • Women losing access to trees, fodder or firewood they relied on.
  • Injuries from explosive remnants of war when land is worked.

How to prevent harm

  • Run free, prior and informed consent on the community’s own terms, and respect a ‘no’.
  • Recognise customary and informal rights before any work starts.
  • Include pastoralists in writing the rules, and keep corridors open.
  • Set up a complaint and dispute route that people trust.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Start with demonstration plots on volunteers’ land and exchange visits. Change nobody’s land rights, and ask for no labour beyond what volunteers offer.

How a pilot could start

  • Farmer-to-farmer exchange visits, so people can see regrowth with their own eyes.
  • Volunteer farmers try it on a small part of their own fields.
  • Farmers and herders write simple community rules on cutting, pruning and grazing together.
  • Count tree survival and harvests together after each season.

What to measure

  • Trees surviving per hectare, counted by farmers and checked with imagery
  • Crop yields and household food security
  • Land and tree disputes raised, and how many were resolved
  • Women’s access to tree products

Evidence behind this bridge

  • How Niger’s FMNR Experience Has Inspired a Global Scaling Movement
  • Rebuilding Resilience in the Sahel: Regreening in the Maradi and Zinder Regions of Niger
  • The Impact of Violent Conflict on Smallholder Agriculture: A Scoping Review
  • Land Restoration From Planting to Proof: A Guide to Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification
  • Voluntary Guidelines on the Responsible Governance of Tenure of Land, Fisheries and Forests (VGGT)
  • Principles for Ecosystem Restoration to Guide the United Nations Decade 2021–2030
  • International Mine Action Standards (IMAS)
  • Programming for Climate, Peace and Security: Thematic Review and Guidance Note

Solar-powered community water for families and schools

Use solar pumps to give families and schools reliable, safe water, run by a committee that fairly represents everyone who uses it.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Where it comes from

Decentralised solar water systems used in humanitarian and rural settings, and water cases in UNDP’s climate solutions for peacebuilding.

Who it could help

Neighbourhoods, settlements and schools where water services were damaged or never existed, and where residents ask for a shared, fairly governed supply.

What must be true first

  • A survey of how much water the source can safely give, and water-quality testing.
  • A water committee with women, displaced families and host residents in real decision-making roles.
  • Spare parts, trained local technicians and a maintenance fund for at least three years.
  • Safe siting away from military positions, with safe, well-lit paths, especially for women and girls.

What could go wrong

  • Armed actors seizing control of the water point or taxing access.
  • Over-pumping that dries wells or springs other people rely on.
  • Some groups being excluded, sparking conflict between host and displaced communities.
  • Unsafe journeys to water, including the risk of gender-based violence.
  • Breakdowns with no parts or funds, leaving people worse off than before.

How to prevent harm

  • Follow Sphere minimum standards for water quantity, quality and access.
  • Run a Do No Harm analysis of who could gain power by controlling water.
  • Never publish exact locations of water points in conflict areas.
  • Offer a confidential complaint channel that bypasses the committee.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Add solar power to one existing, working borehole with an inclusive committee in place, and measure uptime, queues and fairness for six months before expanding.

How a pilot could start

  • Repair or upgrade an existing water point before building a new one.
  • Agree opening hours, fair-use rules and a maintenance plan with users.
  • Train local technicians, including women.
  • Test water quality regularly and share the results in simple terms.

What to measure

  • Days per month the system works (uptime)
  • Litres per person per day, against Sphere’s minimum of 15
  • Queue time and distance for women, girls and people with disabilities
  • Water quality test results
  • Complaints raised and resolved

Evidence behind this bridge

  • The Sphere Handbook: Humanitarian Charter and Minimum Standards in Humanitarian Response
  • Water Under Fire, Volume 3: Attacks on Water and Sanitation Services in Armed Conflict and the Impacts on Children
  • From Crisis to Resilience: Climate Solutions for Positive Peacebuilding
  • Core Humanitarian Standard on Quality and Accountability (2024 edition)
  • Do No Harm (Local Capacities for Peace) Framework
  • State of the Climate in Africa 2025

Shared land agreements and agroforestry for farmer–herder cooperation

Bring farmers and herders together to agree on land, water and routes, plant trees and fodder that benefit both, and train local mediators to settle disputes early.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Where it comes from

Cross-border peacebuilding between Sierra Leone and Guinea, where reported farmer–herder disputes fell sharply but local committees and planted grass had mixed results, plus CGIAR’s climate security assessment tool.

Who it could help

Communities where farming and herding overlap and both groups ask for help to reduce clashes.

What must be true first

  • Consent from both farmers and pastoralists, through representatives each group chooses.
  • Recognised livestock corridors and access to water points.
  • Trusted local mediators, including women.
  • Seasonal calendars of planting, harvest and herd movements.

What could go wrong

  • Committees captured by one group or by local elites. In Sierra Leone only 20.4% said committees work for everyone equally.
  • Planted fodder failing in the dry season, as it did on all five Sierra Leone ranches.
  • Monitoring stopping when outside incentives end.
  • Published route maps exposing herders to raids or theft.

How to prevent harm

  • Track the fairness of committees separately for each group, and act on the results.
  • Choose species with proven dry-season survival in the area.
  • Budget for monitoring after the project ends, owned by local institutions.
  • Keep route maps with the communities, and don’t publish them.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Start with mediated dialogue and a written agreement on one shared corridor or water point, before any planting or construction.

How a pilot could start

  • Hold separate listening sessions with each group, then joint meetings.
  • Agree corridors, crop-damage rules and compensation in writing.
  • Plant drought-hardy fodder and trees in places both groups agree on.
  • Set up an early-warning route so crop damage is reported before it escalates.

What to measure

  • Households reporting a farmer–herder dispute in the past year
  • Share of disputes resolved, and how they were resolved
  • Perceived fairness of committees, by group and gender
  • Fodder and tree survival through the dry season
  • Incomes for both farmers and herders

Evidence behind this bridge

  • Building Cross-Border Peace and Strengthening Sustainable Livelihoods of Cattle Herders and Crop Farmers in Sierra Leone and Guinea: Endline Assessment
  • Climate Security Sensitivity Tool: IPSR Innovation Profile
  • The Impact of Violent Conflict on Smallholder Agriculture: A Scoping Review
  • Climate, Peace and Security in Eastern Chad: Understanding Risks, Strengthening Resilience and Building Lasting Peace
  • Do No Harm (Local Capacities for Peace) Framework
  • Voluntary Guidelines on the Responsible Governance of Tenure of Land, Fisheries and Forests (VGGT)

Home-grown school meals for child-centred recovery

Serve school meals made with food bought from local farmers, so children eat and learn while nearby farms gain a steady market.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Where it comes from

School meal programmes that now reach at least 466 million children worldwide, many of them linked to local food purchasing. A review of 57 studies found modest gains in attendance and growth, though most studies had a high risk of bias.

Who it could help

Schools that are open and safe, in communities that want meals and have farmers able to supply them.

What must be true first

  • Safe school buildings that are not used for military purposes.
  • Clean water, hygiene, and safe food storage and cooking.
  • A child safeguarding policy and trained staff.
  • Fair, transparent purchasing from local farmers and women’s groups.

What could go wrong

  • Schools becoming targets, or meals drawing children into unsafe journeys.
  • Food diverted or sold, or corruption in purchasing.
  • Out-of-school, displaced or disabled children being left out.
  • Firewood for cooking driving tree loss.
  • Meals stopping suddenly when funding ends.

How to prevent harm

  • Follow the Safe Schools Declaration: schools are never used for military purposes.
  • Offer take-home rations for children who can’t attend.
  • Use fuel-efficient stoves and plant woodlots.
  • Run child-friendly, confidential complaint channels.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Pilot in a few safe schools that already have water, buy a few staple foods locally, and plan with the community from day one for when outside funding ends.

How a pilot could start

  • Start in a few schools that have water and safe access.
  • Form a food committee with parents, teachers and farmers.
  • Buy from local farmers through small, transparent contracts.
  • Plan menus with nutrition advice and local foods.

What to measure

  • School days with meals served, against days planned
  • Attendance and retention for girls and boys
  • Dietary diversity of meals
  • Share of food bought from local farmers, including women farmers
  • Food safety incidents and safeguarding reports handled

Evidence behind this bridge

  • State of School Feeding Worldwide 2024
  • Impacts of School Feeding on Educational and Health Outcomes of School-Age Children and Adolescents in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
  • Safe Schools Declaration

  • Global Report on Food Crises 2026
  • The Sphere Handbook: Humanitarian Charter and Minimum Standards in Humanitarian Response

Healing landscapes: psychosocial support woven into restoration work

Combine community restoration work, like tree nurseries, gardens and water care, with basic psychosocial support, so people can recover together while repairing their surroundings.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Where it comes from

The IASC’s layered model of mental health and psychosocial support, which treats community and family supports as a core layer; WHO’s psychological first aid; and WHO’s scalable programmes, Problem Management Plus and Self-Help Plus, which trained and supervised non-specialists delivered in trials in Pakistan and Uganda.

Who it could help

Communities that want shared, practical activities, where trained people can offer basic support and referrals.

What must be true first

  • Facilitators trained in psychological first aid.
  • If you offer a structured programme such as PM+ or Self-Help Plus: helpers trained in it, regular supervision, and materials adapted to the local language and culture.
  • A referral list for specialised mental health care that actually works.
  • Voluntary participation, with no pressure to share experiences.
  • Separate groups where needed (women, men, youth), and child-friendly spaces run by trained staff.

What could go wrong

  • Pushing people to talk about painful events, which can cause harm.
  • Labelling people as ‘traumatised’ or creating stigma.
  • Unpaid work presented as therapy.
  • Raising expectations of care that isn’t available.

How to prevent harm

  • Make no clinical claims. This is support, not treatment.
  • Pay fairly for work, and keep support activities voluntary.
  • Use only validated, locally adapted wellbeing measures, with ethical review.
  • Protect privacy: no names or stories shared without informed consent.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Begin with one nursery or garden group led by trained local facilitators and backed by a tested referral route, before adding any structured wellbeing activities.

How a pilot could start

  • Start a community nursery or garden group that meets regularly.
  • Train group facilitators in psychological first aid: look, listen, link.
  • Agree group rules on confidentiality and respect.
  • Link each group to health and protection services for referrals.
  • Where distress is affecting daily life, offer PM+ or Self-Help Plus through trained, supervised helpers, always as a free choice.

What to measure

  • Voluntary participation and retention
  • Referrals made and completed
  • Plants and trees surviving
  • Participants’ own sense of connection and wellbeing (validated, locally adapted tools only)

Trials show that structured help delivered by trained, supervised non-specialists can reduce distress (PM+ in Pakistan, Self-Help Plus in Uganda). Combining that help with restoration work has not been tested. Treat the combination as an idea to test carefully.

Evidence behind this bridge

  • Guided Self-Help to Reduce Psychological Distress in South Sudanese Female Refugees in Uganda: A Cluster Randomised Trial

Shock-responsive cash for community-chosen restoration

Pay fair wages, through trusted social protection systems, for restoration work the community chooses, so families can buy food while land and water systems recover.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Where it comes from

UNICEF’s 2026 guidance on shock-responsive social protection; a review of 165 studies in which most found that cash transfers contributed to progress on poverty, schooling and health; and climate–peace programme experience reviewed by UNDP.

Who it could help

Households facing hunger or lost income where cash can be delivered safely and local markets still work.

What must be true first

  • Safe payment channels that armed actors can’t tax or control.
  • Fair selection rules that people understand and can challenge.
  • Wages equal to local rates, and no work for children below the legal working age.
  • Support for people who can’t do physical work, such as older people, people with disabilities and pregnant women.

What could go wrong

  • Local elites capturing the beneficiary lists.
  • Payments seen as favouring one group, fuelling tension.
  • Unsafe work on contaminated land.
  • Personal data on beneficiaries exposed or misused.
  • Price rises if local markets can’t supply goods.

How to prevent harm

  • Check that markets can supply goods before using cash.
  • Run explosive ordnance checks before any land work.
  • Minimise payment data, protect it, and delete it when no longer needed.
  • Watch for tensions and adjust selection with the community.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Start with one small, community-chosen project and a short payment cycle, with clear rules and an independent complaint route.

How a pilot could start

  • Let the community choose projects, such as water-harvesting bunds, tree nurseries or soil conservation.
  • Use existing social protection systems where they are safe and trusted.
  • Collect only the personal data needed for payments, and protect it.
  • Publish the selection rules and a complaint route.

What to measure

  • Payments made on time and in full
  • Household food consumption
  • Restoration works still maintained after 12 months
  • Complaints raised and resolved, and inclusion or exclusion errors
  • Protection incidents linked to payments (the target is none)

Cash transfers in general have strong evidence. Paying for community-chosen restoration work in conflict settings has much less, so measure carefully.

Community seed systems for food sovereignty after displacement

Help farmers recover diverse, locally adapted seed and share it fairly, so families can replant after losing harvests, tools and seed stocks.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Where it comes from

Research showing that conflict destroys crops, seed stocks and markets, and that cropland loss can last for years without recovery support.

Who it could help

Farming communities returning to their land, or hosting displaced farmers, who say seed is what stops them replanting.

What must be true first

  • An assessment, with farmers, of whether the problem is seed availability, money to buy it, or seed quality.
  • Varieties farmers know and can save and replant.
  • Working local markets and traders, where they exist.
  • Safe access to fields.

What could go wrong

  • Unsuitable or non-local seed that fails or can’t be saved.
  • Free handouts undercutting local seed traders.
  • Women farmers excluded from seed fairs or banks.
  • Seed banks controlled by a few powerful people.

How to prevent harm

  • Prefer local varieties that farmers choose.
  • Buy locally where markets work.
  • Make sure women and displaced farmers have a voice and access.
  • Keep seed bank records simple, open and local.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Hold a seed needs discussion with farmers, then one community seed fair buying from local suppliers, before any large distribution.

How a pilot could start

  • Ask farmers what seed they need and why they lack it.
  • Support local seed fairs or vouchers that buy from local traders.
  • Help farmer groups set up community seed banks with shared rules.
  • Return seed to the bank after harvest so stocks grow.

What to measure

  • Farmers with enough seed of the varieties they prefer
  • Number of crops and varieties grown
  • Area replanted
  • Women farmers’ access to seed
  • Seed returned to the community bank

  • The Impact of Violent Conflict on Smallholder Agriculture: A Scoping Review

Community-led restoration monitoring for shared, trusted proof

Let communities measure restoration themselves, with simple indicators they choose, checked against satellite images, so results are trusted and owned locally.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Where it comes from

WRI’s monitoring, reporting and verification approach, field-tested with more than 200 locally led restoration projects.

Who it could help

Any community running restoration that wants to show results to itself, funders and authorities without giving up control of its data.

What must be true first

  • Community agreement on what to measure and who may see the data.
  • Simple tools that work offline.
  • A data protection plan: what is collected, where it is stored, who can see it and when it is deleted.
  • Clear rules for location data in conflict areas.

What could go wrong

  • Precise maps or photos revealing homes, people or assets to armed actors.
  • Data used for land grabs or surveillance.
  • Outsiders taking the data and the credit.
  • Monitoring turning into box-ticking for funders.

How to prevent harm

  • Publish only combined, coarse-resolution data.
  • No people, faces or homes in photos without consent, and never children’s faces.
  • Written data agreements that keep the community in control.
  • Keep raw data on local devices and delete what isn’t needed.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Choose three community-defined indicators and fixed photo points without people, and report results only at village or district level.

How a pilot could start

  • Agree indicators with the community, for example trees alive, water flowing, harvests.
  • Train and pay local monitors, including women and young people.
  • Combine field counts with satellite checks at a coarse scale.
  • Share results in community meetings before anyone else sees them.

What to measure

  • Indicators reported on time
  • Community satisfaction with the process
  • Data incidents (the target is none)
  • Decisions changed because of monitoring results

Evidence behind this bridge

  • Land Restoration From Planting to Proof: A Guide to Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification
