Solar power for clinics and maternity care

Give health centres reliable solar power, so they can keep vaccines cold, light night-time births and run basic equipment, with local people trained to look after it.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Where it comes from

WHO and partners found that close to 1 billion people are served by health facilities with unreliable electricity or none. UNDP’s Solar for Health has installed solar power in some 1,000 health centres and storage facilities in 15 countries.

Who it could help

Health centres and maternity units with no power or frequent outages, where the health authority and the community ask for support and trained staff are in place.

What must be true first

  • An energy check with health staff: which equipment needs power, when, and for how long.
  • Agreement with the health authority on who owns the system, who maintains it and who pays for new batteries.
  • Trained local technicians, including women, with spare parts and a maintenance fund for at least five years.
  • Secure installation that does not make the clinic a target for theft.

What could go wrong

  • Systems failing within a few years for lack of maintenance or batteries, leaving clinics worse off than before.
  • Panels or batteries stolen, or armed actors trying to take control of the power supply.
  • Power diverted from health care to other uses.
  • Old batteries dumped where they pollute land and water.

How to prevent harm

  • Budget for maintenance and battery replacement from the start, with the health authority.
  • Keep the clinic open to everyone, whichever group they belong to.
  • Don’t publish exact clinic locations in conflict areas.
  • Plan safe recycling of batteries and panels before installing them.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Power the vaccine refrigerator and maternity lighting at one clinic, with trained local technicians, and track hours of power and repairs for six months before expanding.

How a pilot could start

  • Start with the essentials: the vaccine refrigerator, lights for night-time births, and a few sockets for basic devices.
  • Install and train together, so staff and local technicians understand the system.
  • Keep a simple log of faults, repairs and battery health.
  • Add equipment only once the system has worked reliably for a full season.

What to measure

  • Hours per day with power, and outages per month
  • Days the vaccine refrigerator stays within its safe temperature range
  • Night-time births attended with good light
  • Repairs done by local technicians, and time taken to repair
  • Diesel use avoided

The need is well documented. Evidence on health results after clinics switch to solar comes mostly from programme reporting, not independent evaluations.

Evidence behind this bridge

  • Energizing Health: Accelerating Electricity Access in Health-Care Facilities
  • Solar for Health
  • The Sphere Handbook: Humanitarian Charter and Minimum Standards in Humanitarian Response
  • Core Humanitarian Standard on Quality and Accountability (2024 edition)
  • Do No Harm (Local Capacities for Peace) Framework

Zaï pits and water harvesting to bring dry land back into use

Dig small planting pits filled with compost to catch rain and nutrients, so crops and trees can grow again on hard, degraded dryland fields.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Where it comes from

A traditional technique from the Sahel. Field records from Niger, compiled by WOCAT, show plots with pits and fertiliser yielding about 409 kg of millet per hectare, against 195 kg on control plots.

Who it could help

Hard, degraded dryland fields with less than about 800 mm of rain a year, where households want to farm again and can share the heavy work.

What must be true first

  • Soils that suit pits (not sandy soils or valley bottoms), checked with local farmers.
  • Enough compost or manure, which may mean agreements with herders.
  • Clear rights, so the people who dig and improve the land keep the benefits.
  • Confirmation from a mine action authority that the land is safe to dig, wherever fighting took place.

What could go wrong

  • Heavy digging (40 to 60 person-days per hectare by hand) excluding households short of workers, or falling unfairly on women and children.
  • Improved land attracting claims from more powerful people.
  • Competition with herders for manure and crop residues.
  • Injuries from explosive remnants of war when land is dug.

How to prevent harm

  • Pay fairly or share the work, and never use child labour.
  • Agree in writing who keeps the land and the harvests before work begins.
  • Include herders in agreements on manure and crop residues.
  • Run explosive ordnance checks and risk education before any digging.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Demonstrate pits on a small area of volunteers’ land, with shared tools and work, and compare harvests with neighbouring plots after one season.

How a pilot could start

  • Farmer-to-farmer visits to see working pits.
  • Volunteer households try pits on a small part of their own fields before the rains.
  • Organise shared work groups, so households short of workers are not left out.
  • Compare harvests from pit plots and nearby fields together after each season.

What to measure

  • Area brought back into use
  • Crop yields on pit plots and comparison plots
  • Who did the work: hours by women, men and young people
  • Land disputes raised and resolved

The yield figures come from field records, not controlled trials, and depend on rainfall, compost and labour.

Evidence behind this bridge

  • Zai or Tassa Planting Pits (Niger)
  • Rebuilding Resilience in the Sahel: Regreening in the Maradi and Zinder Regions of Niger
  • How Niger’s FMNR Experience Has Inspired a Global Scaling Movement
  • The Impact of Violent Conflict on Smallholder Agriculture: A Scoping Review
  • International Mine Action Standards (IMAS)
  • Voluntary Guidelines on the Responsible Governance of Tenure of Land, Fisheries and Forests (VGGT)

Safe land release so families can farm again

Work with accredited mine action organisations to confirm which land is safe, so families can return to their fields, with farming support ready when land is handed back.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Where it comes from

The International Mine Action Standards, and GICHD and UNDP analysis that describes safe land as a precondition for development. A global study found that conflict-affected areas lost 23.7% more cropland than comparable areas, with losses lasting for years.

Who it could help

Communities whose farmland, grazing or water points can’t be used because of suspected explosive hazards, and who ask for help to return to them.

What must be true first

  • A national mine action authority or accredited organisation leading all survey and clearance.
  • Community knowledge of where accidents happened, shared only with mine action teams.
  • Agreement on land rights before release, so land returns to the people who used it.
  • Farming support (seed, tools, water) planned to start as land is released.

What could go wrong

  • Released land taken by more powerful people instead of returning to its users.
  • People going back onto land before it has been surveyed.
  • Benefits not reaching everyone equally, as GICHD and UNDP warn.
  • Expecting quick results: survey and clearance can take a long time.

How to prevent harm

  • Only accredited organisations survey and clear land. Restoration teams never do.
  • Agree land rights and priorities with the community before release.
  • Track who benefits from released land, by gender and group.
  • Keep risk education going after land is released.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Ask the mine action authority about survey plans for land the community has prioritised, and run risk education, before any farming support starts.

How a pilot could start

  • Ask the mine action authority what survey has been done and what is planned.
  • Arrange risk education for families, especially children and people who collect firewood or water.
  • Agree with the community which land matters most for food and water.
  • Link released land to seed, tools and farming support.

What to measure

  • Area released for use, as reported by the mine action authority
  • Released land actually farmed or grazed within a year
  • Who uses released land, by gender and group
  • Explosive ordnance accidents (the target is none)

The links between land release and recovery come mostly from analysis and case studies. Measure who actually uses released land.

Evidence behind this bridge

  • International Mine Action Standards (IMAS)
  • Leaving No One Behind: Mine Action and the Sustainable Development Goals
  • Landmine Monitor 2025
  • Armed Conflict Accelerates Cropland Loss and Food Insecurity Worldwide
  • The Impact of Violent Conflict on Smallholder Agriculture: A Scoping Review
  • Voluntary Guidelines on the Responsible Governance of Tenure of Land, Fisheries and Forests (VGGT)

Restoring wetlands and marshes for water, food and shared livelihoods

Help drained or damaged wetlands recover where water can be secured, so fish, reeds, grazing and clean water return for the people who depend on them.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Where it comes from

The Mesopotamian Marshes of Iraq, where more than 40% of the drained marshes were reflooded by 2005 and native species began to return, followed by UNEP-supported monitoring and pilot water and sanitation projects.

Who it could help

Communities that depend on wetlands for fishing, reeds, grazing or water, and ask for help to restore them, where enough water can be secured.

What must be true first

  • A water budget showing that enough water can reach the wetland in dry years, agreed with upstream users.
  • Agreement among fishers, herders, farmers and other users on access and rules.
  • Water-quality testing before people drink the water or eat the fish.
  • Confirmation from a mine action authority that the area is safe, wherever fighting took place.

What could go wrong

  • Restoration failing because upstream dams, drought or irrigation take the water.
  • Disputes between upstream and downstream users, or between user groups.
  • Pollution from oil, waste or sewage harming health.
  • Some users, such as women or displaced families, losing access.

How to prevent harm

  • Secure water first: make no restoration promises without a realistic water budget.
  • Run a Do No Harm analysis of who could gain power by controlling water flows.
  • Share benefits fairly among user groups, with a dispute route they trust.
  • Test water and share the results in simple terms.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Agree a water budget and user rules for one small area, then restore it and monitor water, fish and plants with local users for a full year before expanding.

How a pilot could start

  • Map, with users, who depends on the wetland and how. Keep the map with the community.
  • Agree access rules and seasons with fishers, herders and farmers.
  • Start with small reconnections or water-holding works where water is secured.
  • Monitor water levels, water quality and returning species with local people.

What to measure

  • Area holding water through the dry season
  • Water-quality test results
  • Fish catches and reed or fodder harvests reported by users
  • Disputes between user groups raised and resolved

The marshes began to recover quickly once water returned, but IUCN’s 2025 outlook rates them as critical because water is scarce again. Secure water first.

Evidence behind this bridge

  • Restoring the Garden of Eden: An Ecological Assessment of the Marshes of Iraq
  • Support for Environmental Management of the Iraqi Marshlands 2004–2009
  • The Ahwar of Southern Iraq: Refuge of Biodiversity and the Relict Landscape of the Mesopotamian Cities
  • Principles for Ecosystem Restoration to Guide the United Nations Decade 2021–2030
  • Guidelines on the Protection of the Natural Environment in Armed Conflict
  • Do No Harm (Local Capacities for Peace) Framework

Safer cooking fuel and stoves for displaced families

Provide stoves and fuel chosen with the families who use them, so fewer people breathe smoke, fewer risky trips are made to collect firewood, and less pressure falls on nearby trees.

Evidence: Conceptual · Community: Proposed (unassessed local defaults; use the planner to record reviews)

Where it comes from

WHO’s evidence on household air pollution, and the Women’s Refugee Commission’s work on safe access to fuel and energy in displacement.

Who it could help

Displaced and host families who cook on open fires, where collecting firewood is risky or is straining relations with neighbours.

What must be true first

  • Conversations with women and girls, held separately and safely, about cooking, fuel and the risks of collecting it.
  • Stoves and fuels that suit local food and that local markets can supply.
  • A fuel supply that can last, such as briquettes, local woodlots or gas, planned with host communities.
  • A way to check that stoves are used, and what families spend on fuel.

What could go wrong

  • Stoves that don’t suit local cooking going unused.
  • Families selling food or rations to buy fuel.
  • Tension with host communities over trees and firewood.
  • Claims that stoves alone prevent violence, which they cannot.

How to prevent harm

  • Plan safe access to fuel with protection staff. Never rely on stoves alone to reduce violence.
  • Involve host communities so they benefit from the fuel supply.
  • Choose cleaner fuels where possible, because many wood stoves still produce harmful smoke.
  • Keep information about anyone harmed while collecting fuel confidential, and refer only with consent.

Hazard prerequisite: obtain qualified mine-action assessment for the exact area and intended use before any field intervention. Never inspect or clear suspected ordnance yourself. A checklist is not clearance.

Smaller, safer first step

Hold listening sessions with women and girls, test two or three stove and fuel options with a few volunteer households, and track use, smoke and fuel costs for three months.

How a pilot could start

  • Ask families how they cook, what they burn and what worries them.
  • Test a few stove and fuel options with families before choosing.
  • Plant community woodlots or buy fuel from host communities, so they benefit too.
  • Train local people to make, sell or repair stoves.

What to measure

  • Households still using the stove after six months
  • Time spent collecting fuel, by women, men, girls and boys
  • Money or rations spent on fuel
  • Protection incidents linked to fuel collection (the target is none)
  • Smoke in the home, as families report it

The harm smoke does to health is well established. Evidence that stoves alone make fuel collection safer is limited, so plan protection separately.

Evidence behind this bridge

  • Household Air Pollution
  • SAFE: Safe Access to Fuel and Energy
  • The Sphere Handbook: Humanitarian Charter and Minimum Standards in Humanitarian Response
  • Do No Harm (Local Capacities for Peace) Framework

Bridge Marketplace

A solutions commons: communities share what they need and what they can offer, without prices or financial transactions.

Needed

Water · Food · Restoration · Mediation · Monitoring

Offered

Knowledge · Volunteers · Seeds · Training · Equipment

With JavaScript enabled, create local listings, agree sharing permissions and exchange notices using files. Nothing is uploaded automatically.

Healing and peace practices

Well-established ways of working that keep people safe, support healing and build trust. Use them alongside any bridge. Each one links to the guidance it comes from.

Do No Harm: dividers and connectors

Before and during any project, look at what pulls people apart and what holds them together, and make sure your work strengthens the second.

  1. List the dividers: tensions, grievances, unfair access and anything that separates groups.
  2. List the connectors: markets, water points, shared values, schools and people who bridge groups.
  3. Look at your project’s actions (who gets what, who decides, who is hired) and your team’s behaviour.
  4. Ask how each action affects dividers and connectors, then change what makes things worse.

Take care: Write about issues, not individuals. Don’t name people or armed groups, or record where they are.

Psychological first aid: look, listen, link

Simple, humane support anyone can learn to offer people in distress, without forcing them to talk.

  1. Look: check for safety, urgent basic needs and people who are very distressed.
  2. Listen: approach gently, ask what people need and what worries them, and help them feel calm.
  3. Link: help people meet basic needs, get information, and connect with loved ones and services.

Take care: Never press anyone to describe what happened. Don’t promise what you can’t deliver. Know where to refer people.

Layers of support for mental health and wellbeing

Healing happens in layers: safety and basic services for everyone, community and family support for many, and specialised care for some.

  1. Basic services and security, delivered in ways that protect dignity.
  2. Community and family supports, such as group activities and restored routines.
  3. Focused, non-specialised supports from trained workers.
  4. Specialised services, with referral routes that work.

Take care: Most people recover with good community support. Don’t label people, and don’t start clinical work without qualified staff.

Free, prior and informed consent

People decide for themselves, with full information and no pressure, whether a project goes ahead on their land, and they can say no.

  1. Identify the rights-holders and the representatives they choose.
  2. Map land and resource use together, through participatory mapping.
  3. Share information in local languages and formats, and discuss it over time.
  4. Reach consent through the community’s own process, and agree a complaints mechanism.
  5. Monitor the agreement together and record lessons with the community.

Take care: Consent is not a signature. It can be given in stages, given with conditions, or withdrawn.

Land and tree rights first

Make sure the people who restore land keep the benefits, and that no one loses land or access because of the project.

  1. Recognise all legitimate tenure, including customary, informal and communal rights and women’s use rights.
  2. Consult everyone whose rights may be affected before decisions are made.
  3. Agree in writing who benefits from regrown trees, crops and water.
  4. Provide a fair route to resolve disputes.

Take care: Restoration can raise land values and attract land grabs. Watch for this from the start.

Safe ground: explosive ordnance checks before land work

Land where fighting took place may hide mines or unexploded weapons. Find out before anyone digs, plants or drills.

  1. Ask the national mine action authority or an accredited mine action organisation whether the area has been surveyed.
  2. Arrange explosive ordnance risk education for workers and families before work starts.
  3. Never touch, move or burn suspicious objects. Mark the place and report it.
  4. Stop work immediately if anything suspicious is found.

Take care: Restoration teams never carry out clearance themselves. Only accredited organisations do.

Keep schools safe for learning

Schools are for children. Keep them free from military use and plan school activities so they don’t put children at risk.

  1. Keep schools for learning, never for military or armed security purposes.
  2. Plan safe routes and times for children.
  3. Have a safety and safeguarding plan for every school-based activity.
  4. Report attacks on schools or their military use through appropriate channels.

Take care: Don’t publish school locations or children’s photos from conflict areas.

Women in decision-making

Women have the right to shape decisions about peace and recovery, not just to be consulted at the end.

  1. Hold separate sessions with women at times and places that are safe and convenient, with childcare.
  2. Give women decision-making roles on committees, not token seats.
  3. Check who controls the benefits: water, trees, cash, land.
  4. Partner with local women’s organisations.

Take care: Assess with women themselves whether taking part could expose them to backlash, and plan for it.

Young people as peacebuilders

Young people are partners in building peace, with ideas, energy and a stake in the future.

  1. Invite young people into planning, with real roles and real responsibility.
  2. Create paid, skilled work in restoration, such as nurseries, monitoring and water maintenance.
  3. Support youth-led organisations.
  4. Make reintegration and livelihoods open to young people affected by conflict.

Take care: Don’t treat young people as a security threat, and don’t use them as unpaid labour.

Accountability to the people you serve

People affected by a project should be able to give feedback, complain safely, and see that it changes things.

  1. Ask people how they want to receive information and give feedback.
  2. Set up safe, confidential complaint channels, including for children and for sexual exploitation and abuse.
  3. Respond to every complaint and show what changed.
  4. Share information about the project, its budget and its limits in local languages.

Take care: Complaints about staff misconduct need a protected route that bypasses the staff involved.

Restore with people, not for them

Good restoration is planned and led with local people, uses every kind of knowledge, and is cared for long after the project ends.

  1. Bring in inclusive, participatory decision-making from the very start.
  2. Combine local, Indigenous and scientific knowledge.
  3. Fit the work to the local ecology, culture and economy, and to the wider landscape.
  4. Monitor and adapt during and after the project.

Take care: Planting numbers are not success. Survival, fairness and local ownership are.

Positive peace lens

Peace is more than the absence of violence. It is built by fair institutions, shared resources and trust.

  1. Use the eight pillars as a checklist: which could this bridge strengthen?
  2. Ask which pillars it could weaken, for example through corruption in purchasing.
  3. Choose one or two local signs of change to track over time.

Take care: National peace indices are not designed to judge a single project.

Listen first, and keep listening

Before planning anything, ask people what they need and how they want to be involved. People often ask for smarter help, not more help.

  1. Hold open conversations without a ready-made project to sell.
  2. Ask how people want help delivered, how fast, and who should decide.
  3. Record what you heard in people’s own words, without names.
  4. Report back what you heard and what you will change, and say plainly what you can’t do.

Take care: Listening raises expectations. Be honest about limits, and never collect stories you won’t use or can’t protect.

Scalable psychological help: PM+ and Self-Help Plus

Short, structured WHO programmes that trained non-specialists can deliver, helping adults manage stress, practical problems and low mood.

  1. Adapt the materials to the local language and culture, with local people.
  2. Train helpers, and give them regular supervision.
  3. Offer PM+ one to one or Self-Help Plus in groups, always as a free choice.
  4. Refer anyone who needs specialised care, including anyone at risk of harm, through a referral route that works.

Take care: These programmes need training, supervision and working referrals. They are not treatment for severe conditions, and taking part must never be a condition for receiving aid.

Safe access to fuel and energy

Collecting firewood can expose women and girls to violence. Plan fuel, stoves and energy with them, so cooking puts no one at risk.

  1. Ask women and girls, safely and separately, about fuel needs and risks.
  2. Reduce the need for trips: efficient stoves, cleaner fuels, fuel distributions or local purchase.
  3. Agree safer arrangements with the community, such as going in groups at safer times.
  4. Work with host communities on woodlots and shared rules for using trees.

Take care: Never assume a stove solves a protection problem. Keep survivors’ information confidential, and refer only with their consent.

Community meeting kit

A printable kit for one listening session, made for groups where not everyone reads, writes or speaks the same language.

Everything a facilitator needs to run one listening session with a community that has asked to talk: a session guide, a consent script, picture cards for people who don’t read, voting cards, and a poster that explains how to raise concerns safely. Print it, or copy the text into your own language.

Listening session (About 90 minutes)

  1. Before the day
    • Agree the date, time and place with representatives the community chose itself. Pick a place everyone can reach safely, including women, older people and people with disabilities.
    • Plan separate sessions where people may not speak freely together, for example women, young people, or displaced and host families.
    • Bring a trained interpreter, the printed cards, something to count with (stones, beans or pens) and the complaints poster, already filled in.
    • Know where to refer anyone who needs help before you start, and check that the referral route works.
    • If fighting took place nearby, ask the mine action authority whether the meeting place and the way to it are safe.
  2. Welcome and consent (10 min)
    • Introduce yourselves and your organisation honestly, including what you can’t offer.
    • Read the consent script aloud. Anyone may stay silent, pass or leave at any time.
    • Agree simple ground rules together: one voice at a time, no names of other people, and respect for anyone who passes.
  3. What matters most (20 min)
    • Lay the picture cards on the ground or a table. Explain each one aloud.
    • Each person places three stones or marks on the cards that matter most to them. People may place them privately, one at a time.
    • Count the marks out loud together, so everyone sees the result.

    Questions you could ask:

    • What would make daily life easier?
    • What already works well here that we should protect?
    • What would you like your children to have?
  4. What divides, what connects (20 min)
    • Ask what brings people together here, such as markets, water points, schools or celebrations, and what causes tension.
    • Talk about issues, not individuals. Don’t ask for, or write down, names, homes or exact locations.
    • If the talk becomes heated or painful, hold up the Pause card, take a break and move on.
  5. Ideas and worries (20 min)
    • Describe one or two ideas simply, including what could go wrong and what it would ask of people.
    • People vote with the shape cards: circle for yes, triangle for not sure, square for no. If people prefer, they can vote privately by dropping a card into a bag.
    • A ‘no’ is respected. You may ask what would need to change, but never push.
  6. Closing (10 min)
    • Say honestly what happens next, and when you will come back to report.
    • Explain the ways to raise a concern, and point to the poster.
    • Thank people, and make sure everyone can leave safely.
  7. After the session
    • Record what groups said, never who said it. Use the planner’s consent log for the group’s decision.
    • Don’t keep names. If any notes include names by mistake, destroy them.
    • Report back to the community, in the way it asked for, before sharing anything with anyone else.

Consent script

Read this aloud in the local language. Translate it with people from the community, then have someone else translate it back to check the meaning.

Thank you for coming. We are here to listen, not to decide for you.

Taking part is your choice. You can stay silent, pass, or leave at any time.

Saying no, or leaving, will not change any help or services you or your family receive.

We will not write down your name. We will record what the group says, not who said it.

Please don’t name other people or say where anyone lives.

We will come back to tell you what we heard and what happens next.

You can raise any concern safely, including about us. The poster shows how.

Do you agree to continue?

If children take part

  • Only facilitators trained in child protection run sessions with children.
  • Ask caregivers for consent, and ask each child whether they want to take part. A child’s ‘no’ is respected.
  • Meet in a safe place that others can see, with at least two trained adults present.
  • Use play, drawing and the picture cards. Never ask children about violence or painful events.
  • Know the child protection referral route before the session.

Picture cards

  • Water: Safe water for drinking, cooking, washing and farming
  • Trees: Trees for shade, fruit, fodder and firewood
  • Seeds: Seeds to plant again
  • Farming: Fields, crops and tools
  • Animals and grazing: Grazing, water and routes for animals
  • School: Safe learning for children
  • Health care: A clinic or health worker nearby
  • Cooking fuel: Safe fuel and stoves for cooking
  • Safe land: Land free from explosive hazards
  • Market: A place to buy and sell
  • Work and income: Fair paid work and income
  • Wellbeing: Feeling calm, supported and connected
  • Speak up: A safe way to raise a concern
  • Pause: Stop, or take a break
  • Check results: Measure together what changed

Voting cards

Shapes, not colours, carry the meaning, so the cards work in black-and-white print and for people who see colours differently. The kit avoids thumbs and other hand gestures, which are rude in some cultures.

  • Yes (circle)
  • Not sure (triangle)
  • No (square)

Complaints poster

Something wrong? Tell us safely.

You can raise any worry or complaint, including about our staff.

  • You can talk to: ________________
  • Where: ________________
  • When: ________________
  • Other ways to reach us: ________________
  • Concerns about our staff go to: ________________

You don’t have to give your name. Raising a concern will never affect the help you receive.

Fill in the blanks by hand after printing. Use an organisation’s contact details, never a staff member’s personal phone number.

Bridge planner

Work through a bridge with your community or team, and keep several plans side by side. Answers save on this device only, nothing is sent anywhere, and you can export a backup or a one-page brief at any time. Describe issues and groups, never individuals, and use a general area name rather than an exact location.

The interactive planner needs JavaScript. You can still use its questions on paper or in a meeting:

Consent and voice

  1. Essential: Has the community, through representatives it chose itself, asked for or agreed to this idea?
  2. Essential: Can people say no, or withdraw later, without losing any aid or services?
  3. Have women, young people, displaced families and other often-excluded groups been heard in ways that are safe for them?

Safety and do no harm

  1. Essential: Has a mine action authority or accredited organisation confirmed the land is safe to work, or that it was never contaminated?
  2. Essential: Have you checked that no money, food, water or control will reach armed actors?
  3. Have you mapped what divides and what connects people here, and how this project could affect both?
  4. Is there a safe, confidential way for anyone, including children, to raise a complaint?

Land, water and rights

  1. Essential: Are land, tree and water rights clear enough that the people doing the work will keep the benefits?
  2. If Indigenous Peoples are affected, has a free, prior and informed consent process started on their terms?
  3. Do herders, farmers and other users of the same land or water agree on access and routes?

Ecological fit

  1. Has someone with local knowledge confirmed that rainfall, soil and water can support this?
  2. Will you use native or locally proven species and avoid invasive ones?
  3. Is there a water budget showing the project won’t drain wells or springs that others rely on?

Local ownership and upkeep

  1. Is there a local group, not only an outside organisation, that will run and maintain this?
  2. Are spare parts, skills and money for upkeep planned for at least three years?
  3. Could this start small and grow only if it works?

Measuring and sharing back

  1. Has the community described what success looks like, in its own words?
  2. Will you take a starting measurement (a baseline) before work begins?
  3. Will results be shared back with the community in a usable form, without exposing anyone’s identity or exact location?

Who is in the room?

  • Women
  • Girls and boys (through child-safe methods, with caregivers’ consent)
  • Young people
  • Older people
  • People with disabilities
  • Displaced families
  • Host community
  • Farmers
  • Herders and pastoralists
  • Fishers and wetland users
  • Health workers
  • Indigenous Peoples (where present)
  • Language, religious or ethnic minorities
  • Local authorities
  • Traditional and faith leaders
  • Local organisations, including women’s groups

Impact Metrics Layer

For each relevant indicator, agree a scope, consistent method, baseline, target and review date. Record aggregate observations with dates, sources, confidence and limitations. Missing data is not zero; observed change does not prove causation. Discuss what to keep, adapt, stop or test next. Interactive recording and exports require JavaScript.

Ecological

  • Trees surviving (trees): Count living trees in the same defined planting or regeneration cohort and area. State cohort, assessment age and counting method; do not mix new planting into the original cohort.
  • Soil cover (%): Record points with the locally agreed protective cover (vegetation, litter or mulch) out of all sampled points. Repeat the same transect, season and cover definition.
  • Water retention (mm): Record retained water depth in millimetres using one consistent field protocol. Define soil depth, area, interval after wetting, rainfall and instrument. Do not substitute infiltration rate or compare incompatible methods.
  • Biodiversity observations (distinct taxa): Count distinct species or consistently identified taxonomic groups observed in a fixed survey area and effort. Record season, duration and identification limits. This is observed richness, not a complete biodiversity index.

Community

  • Participation rate (%): Count unique consenting participants against the agreed eligible group for the same period. Define participation and eligibility; repeat attendees count once. Keep only aggregate totals.
  • Women leadership % (%): Use community-agreed meaningful decision-making positions. Count positions consistently and report vacancies and representation limits in notes. Representation alone does not demonstrate influence.
  • Youth leadership % (%): Define the local youth age range and meaningful leadership roles. Count the same positions over time. Youth and women can overlap; these percentages must not be added together.
  • Community trust indicators (%): Choose one locally reviewed, anonymous trust question and a fixed positive-response rule. Record wording, response scale, sampling and non-response. This is a local proxy, not a validated universal trust score.

Peace

  • Disputes resolved (disputes): Count disputes considered resolved by the parties through a voluntary process in a defined reporting period. State the follow-up rule and recurrence. More resolutions may reflect more disputes; do not interpret the count alone as more peace.
  • Shared projects created (projects): Count distinct projects jointly initiated by the locally defined groups during the reporting period. Define what qualifies as shared and created; do not double-count a project across groups.
  • Connector institutions strengthened (institutions): Count institutions meeting locally agreed evidence criteria for stronger cooperation, such as joint decisions, inclusive access and accountable shared resources. Record the criteria and review process; attendance alone is insufficient.

Wellbeing

  • Food security (%): Use a fixed locally reviewed food-sufficiency question and recall period, for example the previous seven days. Record wording and season. This local proxy is not a clinical assessment or a standardized food-security classification.
  • School attendance (%): Use aggregate attendance for the same eligible learner group and reporting period. Document closures and exclusions. Do not store children's names or individual attendance records.
  • Service access (%): Choose one specified service, eligibility rule and recall period. Define accessible, affordable and usable with the community. Do not combine unrelated services or record facility locations.

Community Knowledge Capture

Record community observations, lessons learned and unexpected outcomes with local context, a collective source, date, review process, differing views and sharing permission. Local-only accounts stay out of shared summaries but remain in private backups. Interactive capture and exchange require JavaScript.

72 illustrative community knowledge prompts — not verified findings

These invented examples are discussion prompts, not evidence about actual communities. Record your own locally supported account.

Seed sovereignty & nurseries

  • Community observations: “A seed-bank group recorded separate balances and losses for each variety.” Prompt: Which records, dates and verification support this account, and what remains missing?
  • Lessons learned: “Tracking nursery survival separately from germination changed the next water-supply plan.” Prompt: What denominators and observation dates were used, and what alternative explanations remain?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “A successful seed distribution reduced demand for a locally valued variety.” Prompt: Who chose the varieties, whose preferences were overlooked and how can diversity be protected?

Shared watersheds

  • Community observations: “Upstream and downstream groups continued their maintenance review through a dry season.” Prompt: What period and attendance support this account, whose concerns remained unresolved, and did water access change?
  • Lessons learned: “Discussing downstream costs before choosing erosion works changed the pilot design.” Prompt: Whose input changed the decision, and which impacts still need monitoring?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “A successful water-retention trial raised concerns about downstream availability.” Prompt: What measurements and seasonal conditions support the concern, and what independent review is needed?

Shared seed systems

  • Community observations: “Seed stewards from two communities compared germination results using an agreed method.” Prompt: Were samples and conditions comparable, and were failed trials included?
  • Lessons learned: “Agreeing crop-failure provisions reduced uncertainty about seed replenishment obligations.” Prompt: Who found the provisions fair, who disagreed, and what evidence supports the change?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Interest in an exchanged variety reduced demand for a locally valued seed.” Prompt: Which preferences changed, and how can local diversity and farmer choice be protected?

Cross-border restoration

  • Community observations: “Partner groups completed a joint review of their separate restoration pilots.” Prompt: What commitments were reviewed, which gaps remained, and could participants safely disagree?
  • Lessons learned: “Parallel local pilots allowed ecological learning while travel arrangements remained unresolved.” Prompt: Which learning could be shared, and what limitations did separate implementation introduce?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Different funding cycles left one partner unable to maintain its pilot.” Prompt: How were responsibilities renegotiated without blame or unequal obligations?

Joint monitoring

  • Community observations: “Two monitoring teams found different soil-cover estimates and documented the discrepancy.” Prompt: What sampling effort, method and conditions could explain the difference?
  • Lessons learned: “Keeping disputed interpretations in the report helped partners continue the review.” Prompt: Who felt heard, who did not, and did the review affect any decision?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Publishing comparisons was interpreted as ranking one community against another.” Prompt: What feedback identified this effect, and what presentation would preserve learning without unfair comparison?

Offline education hubs

  • Community observations: “Learners completed the selected lessons during an Internet outage.” Prompt: Which lessons, period and failed attempts were recorded, and who could not access a device?
  • Lessons learned: “A rotating device schedule made supported learning sessions easier to attend.” Prompt: Whose access improved, whose declined, and what did facilitators observe beyond attendance?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Keeping the hub open longer increased unpaid work for educators.” Prompt: What workload and compensation arrangements need review?

Community archives

  • Community observations: “The stewardship group restored its trial collection from a separate backup.” Prompt: Was every item readable, and were permissions and catalogue context also recovered?
  • Lessons learned: “Reviewing permissions item by item clarified which accounts should stay private.” Prompt: Who authorized each decision, and how can knowledge holders revise it?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “A shared historical account prompted disagreement between generations.” Prompt: How can differing accounts be preserved without deciding which group owns the only valid history?

Local knowledge systems

  • Community observations: “Growers corrected a translated account before approving a summary.” Prompt: What meaning changed, and were differences of interpretation kept visible?
  • Lessons learned: “Returning observations in local language helped the group revise its planting trial.” Prompt: How did the account inform a decision, and what other evidence or constraints mattered?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “An approved summary was reused beyond its intended context.” Prompt: What permissions were misunderstood, and what correction or withdrawal is possible for copies already shared?

Mesh communication

  • Community observations: “Local resource requests succeeded while the Internet uplink was disconnected.” Prompt: How many attempts succeeded, which services failed, and under what power and test conditions?
  • Lessons learned: “Training a second maintenance role shortened recovery during a trial outage.” Prompt: What comparison supports this, and what specialist assistance was still needed?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Replacement batteries cost more than the pilot budget allowed.” Prompt: What lifecycle costs were omitted and which simpler options should be reconsidered?

Resilience information portals

  • Community observations: “Residents identified an expired information page during an offline trial.” Prompt: Were dates clear, which copies remained in circulation, and how was the correction communicated?
  • Lessons learned: “Providing a spoken version helped participants find the agreed information.” Prompt: Whose access improved and which language or disability barriers remain?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “More requests for updates exceeded the volunteer editorial group’s capacity.” Prompt: Which information should be prioritized, retired or supported by additional resources?

Regenerative Governance

  • Community observations: “Assembly participants could explain why one maintenance proposal was selected over another.” Prompt: Who was asked, who was absent, and could people challenge the reasons without retaliation?
  • Lessons learned: “Separating spending approval from expenditure checks helped the council identify an unexplained cost.” Prompt: What changed after review, and what alternative explanations or conflicts of interest remain?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Publishing meeting dates increased attendance but also increased unpaid care burdens for some participants.” Prompt: Which groups faced new burdens, and what timing, access or compensation arrangements did they propose?

Natural regeneration

  • Community observations: “Households reported protecting naturally regenerated trees through two dry seasons.” Prompt: Which cohort, how were surviving trees checked, and were all land users represented?
  • Lessons learned: “Discussing tree rights before pruning helped clarify shared expectations.” Prompt: What was agreed about use and ownership, and which disagreements remain unresolved?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Tree ownership became contentious after crop prices rose.” Prompt: Whose claims changed, what alternative explanations exist, and what voluntary review is needed?

Solar water

  • Community observations: “Water users reported shorter waits after agreeing a shared collection schedule.” Prompt: What periods were compared, how were waits estimated, and who still faced delays?
  • Lessons learned: “Publishing maintenance costs helped residents discuss repair contributions.” Prompt: Who could read or hear the information, and did households unable to pay feel pressured?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “The new pump increased demand faster than the local maintenance group expected.” Prompt: What indicates rising demand, and what limits or maintenance changes need local review?

Farmer–herder cooperation

  • Community observations: “Grazing corridor agreement remained stable for 18 months.” Prompt: How was stability observed across seasons, whose accounts differ, and what counts as a breach?
  • Lessons learned: “Committee elections reduced conflict.” Prompt: What changed after the elections, what else changed, and do all groups agree? Describe association rather than assuming causation.
  • Unexpected outcomes: “A new water point shifted herds toward fields outside the agreed corridor.” Prompt: Which routes changed, who bore the costs, and how could the agreement adapt without identifying households?

School meals

  • Community observations: “Caregivers described more regular school attendance during the meal programme.” Prompt: Which school-open periods were compared, and do aggregate attendance records support the account?
  • Lessons learned: “Rotating meal-planning discussions brought more caregivers into decisions.” Prompt: Who gained a voice, who was absent, and did participation create unpaid work?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Local food purchases increased some prices near the school market.” Prompt: What price observations exist, what seasonal changes occurred, and who was affected?

Healing landscapes

  • Community observations: “Participants described the community garden as a place where they felt comfortable meeting.” Prompt: Was feedback voluntary and anonymous, and did anyone find the space uncomfortable or inaccessible?
  • Lessons learned: “Offering quiet and group activities let people choose how to participate.” Prompt: What preferences were expressed, and which access or support needs remain unmet?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Some residents felt excluded when garden sessions overlapped with caregiving hours.” Prompt: Which scheduling options did residents suggest without naming individuals or recounting trauma?

Cash for restoration

  • Community observations: “Workers said predictable payment dates made household planning easier.” Prompt: Which payment periods were covered, and were delays or excluded workers also heard?
  • Lessons learned: “A public explanation of selection criteria helped clarify eligibility questions.” Prompt: Were criteria understood through accessible formats, and could people challenge decisions safely?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Paid restoration work reduced attendance at an unpaid local maintenance activity.” Prompt: What changed in time use and incentives, and how could community priorities be discussed?

Community seeds

  • Community observations: “Growers reported that a locally preferred seed variety performed well during a dry spell.” Prompt: What plots and season support the account, and were unsuccessful crops also recorded?
  • Lessons learned: “Keeping several varieties allowed growers to compare results before choosing.” Prompt: Who selected varieties, what traits mattered, and how did results vary across soils?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Demand for one successful variety reduced attention to other locally valued seeds.” Prompt: What was lost or gained, and which seed-keeping preferences need renewed discussion?

Community monitoring

  • Community observations: “Residents continued submitting observations after results were discussed in open meetings.” Prompt: How many reporting periods were covered, and whose contributions were still missing?
  • Lessons learned: “Returning findings in local language made it easier for residents to correct errors.” Prompt: Which corrections were made, and could people disagree without consequences?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “A public results board was interpreted as ranking neighbourhoods against each other.” Prompt: How did residents describe the effect, and what less competitive presentation would they prefer?

Solar for clinics

  • Community observations: “Health workers reported fewer interruptions to agreed essential services after a power upgrade.” Prompt: What service periods and outage records support this, without recording patient information or facility locations?
  • Lessons learned: “Training more than one maintenance role helped cover staff absences.” Prompt: Which maintenance tasks could be handled locally, and what specialist support was still required?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Reliable power brought requests for additional equipment beyond the system's capacity.” Prompt: How were priorities and capacity limits explained, and who participated in deciding?

Zaï pits

  • Community observations: “Farmers observed that planting pits retained moisture longer than nearby untreated ground.” Prompt: How and when was moisture observed, and were soil and rainfall conditions comparable?
  • Lessons learned: “Working in small groups made the initial digging effort easier to organize.” Prompt: Who contributed labour, who could not, and was participation voluntary and fairly recognized?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Improved plots attracted grazing that damaged some emerging plants.” Prompt: What observations support this, and which crop and livestock users should discuss adaptations?

Safe land release

  • Community observations: “Residents reported greater confidence using land after formal release and community information sessions.” Prompt: Distinguish perceived confidence from official clearance evidence; never infer safety from informal observations.
  • Lessons learned: “Explaining the formal release process helped residents ask questions about permitted land use.” Prompt: Which questions remained, and how were people directed to qualified mine-action authorities?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Renewed access revealed overlapping land-use claims that had not been discussed before release.” Prompt: What rights and consent processes are needed without publishing locations or naming claimants?

Wetland restoration

  • Community observations: “Fishers reported seeing more young fish during the agreed monitoring season.” Prompt: What survey effort, water conditions and species-identification limits affect this account?
  • Lessons learned: “Including fishers and grazing users in water discussions made trade-offs more visible.” Prompt: Whose priorities were heard, and which water-sharing disagreements remain?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Restored wet areas changed access routes used by some residents.” Prompt: Who reported access difficulties, and what adaptations would protect both habitats and livelihoods?

Safer cooking

  • Community observations: “Participants reported spending less time collecting fuel after trying the new cooking option.” Prompt: What time estimates and season were compared, and did all household members share the benefit?
  • Lessons learned: “Cooking familiar meals during demonstrations helped households judge whether the option suited them.” Prompt: Which preferences and costs mattered, and could households decline without losing support?
  • Unexpected outcomes: “Replacement parts were harder to obtain than the initial trial had suggested.” Prompt: What supply constraints emerged, and which locally maintainable alternatives should be considered?

Methods

How evidence is judged, how ideas are tested for fit, how to measure results without putting anyone at risk, and how translations are checked. Each method opens with a plain summary.

Evidence strength and uncertainty

Say how sure we are, and why.

Set Reading level to Full detail under Display to read the full method.

Grade A means independently replicated measured outcomes. Grade B means a rigorous single study, a large-data analysis or a review of many studies. Grade C means case studies, programme experience or before-and-after results without a comparison group. Grade D means a proposal or hypothesis. Guidance, standards and law are marked “How-to”, and situation reports are marked “Context”, because neither tests whether something works.

Never present targets or plans as achieved results. For every figure, record the publication date, the measurement period, the place, the method and the likely confounders. A publication date is not the date an impact was observed.

Ecological transferability

Will this work with this land, water and climate?

Set Reading level to Full detail under Display to read the full method.

Compare the origin and the proposed site on agro-ecological zone, rainfall, soil, native biodiversity, water budget, land tenure, grazing routes, invasive species risk, climate projections, labour and long-term maintenance. Prefer locally validated species and traditional knowledge. Where conditions differ, design a small trial rather than assuming results will travel.

Peace-positive evaluation

Does this reduce tension, or could it add to it?

Set Reading level to Full detail under Display to read the full method.

Use participatory conflict mapping, the Do No Harm dividers-and-connectors analysis, inclusive consent, analysis of who holds power, and a working dispute-resolution route. Track unintended effects. Look at how benefits and burdens fall on women, children, displaced residents, farmers, pastoralists, people with disabilities and minorities. The positive peace pillars help name lasting changes worth tracking.

Measurement and verification

Measure what the community says matters, and check it honestly.

Set Reading level to Full detail under Display to read the full method.

Combine community-defined outcomes with field surveys, baselines, comparison areas where ethical, coarse-scale remote sensing and clear uncertainty ranges. Useful measures include safe-water functionality, dietary diversity, school attendance, vegetation survival, household income, complaints and conflict incidents. Publish only combined figures that cannot identify a person, household or facility.

Funding and procurement integrity

Make sure money reaches people, not armed groups or middlemen.

Set Reading level to Full detail under Display to read the full method.

Require beneficial-ownership checks, sanctions screening, independent procurement, safeguarding policies, audit trails and controls against diversion. Never trade humanitarian access for political endorsement or favourable publicity. Budget from the start for fair pay, safeguarding and complaints, monitoring, upkeep and a contingency, and publish budgets in summary so communities can see where money goes.

Data ethics and location minimisation

Collect less, protect it, delete it.

Set Reading level to Full detail under Display to read the full method.

Collect only what a decision needs. Record places at the coarsest level that still works, such as district rather than GPS point. Keep raw data on local devices under community agreement, protect it, and set a deletion date. Never publish precise locations of at-risk people, schools, shelters, clinics or water points. Photos should not show faces or homes without informed consent, and never children’s faces in conflict settings. Consent logs record groups and their decisions, never named individuals.

Translation and review

Interface words can be drafted quickly. Safety words must be checked by people.

Set Reading level to Full detail under Display to read the full method.

Language packs have two levels. A draft pack translates only interface words such as buttons and headings. Safety guidance, consent text, legal text and content stay in English until a pack is marked reviewed, with the name of the community group or organisation that checked it and the date. Never machine-translate safety or consent text without review by people who speak the language, ideally from the communities who will use it.

Each content translation records the English it was made from. If the English changes, the old translation is not shown until it is updated. Every pack has a fingerprint, so two groups can confirm they have identical text by comparing a few characters. Translate the consent script with people from the community, then have someone else translate it back to check the meaning.

Research and development opportunities

Promising ideas to test, not proven solutions.

Set Reading level to Full detail under Display to read the full method.

Candidates for careful evaluation include decentralised solar power for water and clinics, farmer-managed natural regeneration and zaï pits in post-conflict areas, wetland restoration where water can be secured, climate-security sensitivity tools, causal impact evaluation, privacy-preserving satellite verification of restoration, local-language knowledge exchange, community seed systems after displacement, scalable psychological help alongside restoration work, safer cooking energy, and conflict-sensitive cash and social protection. Treat emerging technologies as things to evaluate, not established solutions.

Zero Harm and Anti-Coercion covenant

These commitments apply to everyone who uses this tool and every bridge it describes. They are not optional, and no funding, deadline or partnership outweighs them.

Protect identities and locations

Never identify vulnerable individuals, publish the precise locations of at-risk children, families or facilities, or collect information that could be used to find, profile or pressure anyone.

Aid is never a bargaining chip

Support is impartial and independent. It is never conditional on taking part, political or religious loyalty, unpaid labour, information about others, or appearing in publicity. People can say no or withdraw without losing anything.

Nothing for armed actors

No money, goods, water, land or control may be routed to armed actors, and no project may be run in a way that strengthens their hold over civilians.

Safe ground before work

No digging, planting, drilling or clearing on land affected by fighting until a mine action authority or accredited organisation confirms it is safe.

Children first

Follow child safeguarding policies, keep schools free from military use, never use children’s images or stories without informed consent from the child and caregiver, and never in ways that could identify them.

Land and resource justice

Screen every proposal for displacement, dispossession, greenwashing, retaliation and resource conflict. Seek free, prior and informed consent, and respect a no.

Honesty about evidence

Never present a target as a result, a proposal as proven, or a partner’s endorsement that has not been given. Listing a publication here does not mean its authors endorse this tool.

Listen and answer

Every bridge needs a safe, confidential complaint route, including for children and for sexual exploitation and abuse, and a visible response.

Your language, checked by people

Safety, consent and legal text is translated only through language packs reviewed by people who speak the language. A draft translation never changes it.

What this tool will never do

  • Store or show maps of vulnerable people, facilities or routes.
  • Rank, score or profile communities or individuals.
  • Send your plans, searches or settings anywhere. There are no accounts, analytics or trackers.
  • Load code, fonts or images from other websites.
  • Translate safety or consent text automatically, without review by people who speak the language.

Glossary

Plain-language meanings for the terms used on this page.

Agroforestry
Growing trees together with crops or livestock on the same land, so each helps the other.
Baseline
A measurement taken before work starts, so you can see later what changed.
Bridge (in this tool)
A proposal to adapt something that worked in one place for a community elsewhere that asks for it. It stays a proposal until it has been tested there.
Clean cooking
Cooking with fuels and stoves that produce little harmful smoke, such as electricity, gas, biogas or solar.
Community assembly
An accessible forum for affected people to discuss choices, hear different views and make or advise decisions under agreed rules. Attendance alone is not consent.
Conflict sensitivity
Understanding the conflict around you and making sure your work reduces tension rather than adding to it.
Connectors and dividers
Connectors bring people together, like shared markets or values. Dividers pull them apart, like unfair access or old grievances.
Consent log
A record of when a group agreed, agreed with conditions, paused or said no, and when to check again. It records groups, never named individuals.
Contingency
Money set aside in a budget for things that go wrong or cost more than expected.
Decision record
A short account of the options considered, reasons for a choice, responsible role and review date. It should communicate decisions without exposing confidential complaints or personal identities.
Do No Harm
A method for checking how help can accidentally fuel conflict, and for changing course so it builds peace instead.
Elite capture
When a few powerful people take control of a project’s benefits meant for everyone.
Evidence strength
How much weight you can put on a source’s main claims. This tool uses A (strong) to D (untested here).
Explosive ordnance
Mines, unexploded bombs, shells and other explosive remnants of war that can stay dangerous for decades.
Explosive ordnance risk education
Teaching people how to recognise, avoid and report explosive hazards.
FMNR
Farmer-managed natural regeneration: helping trees regrow from living stumps, roots and seeds already in the soil.
FPIC
Free, prior and informed consent: people’s right to decide, without pressure and with full information, whether a project affecting their land goes ahead.
Grievance mechanism
A safe way for people to raise complaints and get a response.
Home-grown school feeding
School meals made with food bought from local farmers.
International humanitarian law
The rules of war that protect civilians, people no longer fighting, and the natural environment.
Land release
The process, run by mine action organisations, of confirming through survey or clearance that land is safe and handing it back for use.
Land tenure
The rules, written or customary, about who can use land, for how long and under what conditions.
Location minimisation
Recording places only as precisely as you truly need, so data can’t be used to find or target people.
MHPSS
Mental health and psychosocial support: any support that protects or improves people’s wellbeing and mental health.
MRV
Monitoring, reporting and verification: measuring results, sharing them and checking they are true.
Participatory budgeting
A process in which people affected by a project help decide how an agreed portion of its resources will be used. The scope, eligibility and decision rules should be clear before proposals are invited.
Pastoralism
Raising livestock on open land, often moving herds with the seasons to find water and grazing.
Positive peace
The attitudes, institutions and structures that create and sustain peaceful societies.
Problem Management Plus (PM+)
A WHO programme of five sessions in which trained non-specialists help adults manage stress and practical problems.
Psychological first aid
Humane, practical support for people in distress: look, listen and link them to help.
Remote sensing
Measuring changes on the ground, such as tree cover, from satellite or aerial images.
Risk register
A list of what could go wrong, how likely and how serious each risk is, who watches it and what will reduce it.
Safeguarding
Everything an organisation does to keep children and adults safe from harm, abuse and exploitation by its staff and activities.
Self-Help Plus
A WHO group course for managing stress, using recorded audio and an illustrated guide, led by trained facilitators.
Shock-responsive social protection
Support systems, such as cash transfers, designed to scale up quickly when a crisis hits.
Stewardship council
A community-mandated group responsible for ongoing care of shared resources, with defined duties, review dates, accountability and a way to replace its members.
Transhumance
The seasonal movement of herders and livestock between grazing areas.
Value chain
All the steps a product goes through, from farm to buyer.
Water budget
An estimate of how much water an area receives and how much can be used without running out.
Zaï pits
Small planting pits filled with compost that catch rain and nutrients on hard, dry soils.

Your data and offline use

Everything you type stays in this browser on this device. Nothing is uploaded. Clearing your browser data deletes it, so export a backup of anything important.

Enable JavaScript to manage private knowledge records on this device.

What is stored here

  • Your display and language settings.
  • Your bridge plans, each with up to five earlier saved versions.
  • An offline copy of this app’s own files, when it is served from a website.

Offline and install

Served from a website, this app keeps a copy of its own files so it opens without a connection. Opened directly from a folder, everything works except the offline copy and installing.

External sources are never copied or cached. Opening one needs a connection.

About and credits

Regenerative Peace Bridges is part of the Planetary Restoration Archive, built by Foster + Navi. It connects documented regenerative work with communities affected by conflict through context-sensitive, independently governed proposals that put children, safe water, food, education, health, land rights and community consent first.

New in version 3

  • Eighteen newly checked sources (49 in total) and five new bridges: solar power for clinics, zaï pits, safe land release, wetland restoration and safer cooking.
  • A community meeting kit: a 90-minute listening session guide, a consent script to read aloud, picture cards, shape-coded voting cards and a complaints poster, ready to print.
  • A deeper planner: several plans side by side, a timeline, a budget with integrity checks, a risk register with a likelihood and impact grid, and a consent log that pauses a plan when a group says no.
  • Language packs: draft French, Spanish and Arabic interfaces, right-to-left layouts, and tools to import, check, export and translate packs. Safety and consent text changes only through reviewed packs.

Future extensions

These are planned and not yet built. Nothing on this page pretends otherwise.

  • Future extension Reviewed language packs made with communities, starting with languages requested by users.
  • Future extension Audio recordings of the consent script, made by native speakers, for people who don’t read.
  • Future extension Sharing a plan directly between two devices, only with both people’s consent and with encryption.
  • Future extension Coarse, location-minimised map layers for planning at district level.
